I inferred from the minister's statement last week that he was opposed to the idea of the Veterans' Land Act being used as a solution to the housing problems of returned veterans. I thought that was what the minister implied in his statement, and I think I was right, since he nods in agreement. I take exception to that, and if the minister feels that his department should not be saddled with the housing problems of veterans, what further positive liaison is carried on with other federal departments? What is being done there?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I entirely agree with my hon. friend in regard to that, and I also agree with the hon. member for Melfort, who belongs to his own political philosophy group over there, that the basic idea of the Soldier Settlement Act and the Veterans' Land Act is settlement on land. The housing feature of it is really an ancillary feature which has developed as being the most popular view. Twenty-seven hundred houses are being constructed at the present time, and six thousand are projected for next year. While I agree with my hon. friend that these should be constructed, and must be constructed, the other question is, who should be in active direction of that policy? Speaking personally I feel strongly that all the housing activities of the administration should be coordinated under one central authority. I believe that is the most effective thing that could be done. So long as I am in charge of the small holdings policy the houses will go on, but I do say to my hon. friend that housing is not the essential feature of the Veterans' Land Act; it is settlement on farms.
I agree with the minister, but the point I am trying to bring out, is 'that someone in the cabinet must press for that coordination to be undertaken, and 'as I see it, it is his duty to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think my bon, friend can trust me to that extent.

With regard to small holdings, I know of a man who returned and wanted to get on some land. Because of his age he was not recommended; his application under the Veterans' Land Act was turned down. He then decided to make a second proposal, stating that he would like to settle himself at a filling station on one of the
highways and take in a piece of land consisting of six or seven acres. Under the terms of the act would that be called a small holding?

He made his application, and they turned him down on that account. They said, "Oh, well, you have not a permanent income."

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If he had reasonable prospects of a reasonable income, that would be enough.
The letter I received from the soldier settlement board was to this effect-

What can be done about returned soldiers who have land of their own and have difficulty in getting machinery? I know that the veterans department had a large quantity of machinery placed on priority. Many of those veterans do not come under the Veterans' Land Act because their parents own the farm and are giving the land to the veterans. The result is they do not know where to go. Would the minister give us a statement to clear that up?

I realize that time is important, but this is an * occasion on which most hon. members wish to add a word to the discussion. We are grateful to that group of men who have played such a tremendous part in the fight for our very existence. I can assure you, sir, that I shall be brief, but there are a few observations I should like to make and some information I should like to obtain from the minister.
I have information to the effect that even a boy bom on a farm, who enlisted at eighteen or eighteen and a half years of age and now comes back seeking to acquire a farm home-

stead or other land, has not within the meaning of the act the necessary qualifications for the assistance that is granted under the act. Will the department give consideration to amendments to make it practicable for the farmer's son to come within the meaning of the act? I am not sure whether the minister's department is charged with this responsibility. I now refer to veterans who have married British girls overseas, and whose wives are still detained in the old land. There are some pathetic cases. I know it is very difficult to do anything about them, yet I do make an appeal on their behalf. I know of young veterans being returned to Canada for discharge from the army, whose wives in the old country are expecting children, and they are anxious that these children should be bom in Canada. Yet under the act they cannot be moved except within a certain time limit. I do hope the department are giving consideration to this serious situation and will try to bring these wives to Canada in order that their children may be bom here.
I should like to say a word with respect to the veterans guard, about which I believe there was some discussion this morning. I have a sympathetic feeling for these veterans of two wars who have made a tremendous contribution and now are too old to take advantage of many of the rehabilitation measures provided for their benefit. I should like the minister to say his department is giving serious consideration to some action that will satisfy the veterans of two wars who have been serving in internment camps or elsewhere but who now, at the age of fifty-five or more, do not care to take on obligations which will extend for another twenty years.
I do not think I would be fair if I did not take just a few minutes to say that I for one indeed appreciate the sympathetic and serious approach of the minister to these problems. I have had occasion to bring to his attention matters which I know do not come within his department, but he has always listened to me and sincerely tried to help. I believe we all appreciate his sympathetic understanding, and that is something the veterans will need possibly more than anything else in the world. After all, though there may be thousands of veterans, no two of them will have problems exactly the same. This afternoon we see how well the minister deals with these matters; he listens to our remarks and waits for any suggestions that may be made which will be of assistance to the returned men.
I want to refer to another matter, and in doing so I hope I shall not be misunderstood; for that happens so easily. For instance, I believe it was reported in a Canadian press

Supply-Veterans Affairs
dispatch that the members had voted themselves an additional indemnity of $2,000 for the session, and of course that is absolutely wide of the mark. I hope no deputation is waiting for me to collect mine when I get home, because actually we shall only get about $640 per annum above our expenses. 1 want to refer to the matter raised this morning by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, the relief allowance of $25 a week. We should all like to see the people of this country everywhere in receipt of $25 a week, but I want to take a realistic and practical view of this suggestion. I say to you, Mr. Chairman, and to this committee, that the moment we raise the allowance to such a level that a man has no desire to work, wTe are not doing him any good. In my opinion no man is happy unless he is employed. Employment is the greatest source of security, and I should like to see full employment at substantial wages. But I constantly ask myself whether we should offer a man a reward that will take away from him the desire to forage for himself. I suggest that to the committee as something to consider.
The last matter I have in mind has to do with the widows of service men; something I have brought up in the house on previous occasions. I should like to know from the minister whether anything has been done to see that a widow is given the reestablishment credit which her deceased husband would have received if he had come back. This is a very important matter, inasmuch as many of these soldiers married shortly before they went away, and some left small families. Many of these people are living in quarters that cannot be considered either comfortable or secure. I believe the reestablishment of a widow and her young family is just as important, in many ways, as the reestablishment of a soldier who has returned from overseas. I should like to know whether anything definite has been done with respect to granting the reestablishment credit to the widow of a member of the armed forces in order that she may be able to reestablish herself and her family.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I want to thank my
hon. friend for his constructive observations, which I think I can deal with in a very few minutes.
In the first place he mentioned the boys on farms, and thought this limitation in regard to eighteen years of age was unfair. As the regulation now is being administered by the director I believe that if the lad has had two years of actual practical experience on a farm he can qualify under the provisions of the
Veterans' Land Act. From my own memories I know that any lad who has been brought up on a farm and done the work of a farm is pretty well qualified to look after a farm himself after he gets older, so I agree in large part with my hon. friend in that regard.
The hon. gentleman dealt with the early return of the wives of veterans. A declaration in that connection was made yesterday or the day before by my colleague the Minister of National Defence, so I need not deal further with that point. The hon. gentleman went on to speak of the veterans of both wars, and made a most commendable suggestion in their behalf. May I tell him that we are now establishing a special directorate in the Department of Veterans Affairs to deal with the problem of the veterans of both wars.
Then my hon. friend went on to mention the reestablishment credit for widows. I am sorry that I am perhaps reactionary in regard to that matter. I remember when we had our committee dealing with this problem. Rightly or wrongly-it is a matter for the committee and the members of the house to decide later-we came to the conclusion that war service grants and gratuities are largely the expression of a nation's gratitude to the men who served the country in time of war. We treated the credits as a conjunct function combining in the first place the same ideas but essentially combining them over a ten-year period with reestablishment as such, and relating it to the national economy, and belonging particularly to the individual who had returned to Canada and was being reestablished. That may be the wrong idea, but it was the basic idea behind that provision. I doubt very much, and I say this without hesitation, the advisability of extending the reestablishment credit to anyone except the ex-service man who comes back to Canada and seeks to rebuild a home for himself or herself, because it applies also to women. I believe those were the main points raised by the hon. gentleman, and I thank him very much for them.
Will the minister pursue that matter a little farther? I know of some unfortunate instances.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It will come up for discussion when the Pension Act will be considered by the veterans affairs committee, I imagine about next March.

I have been a member of this veterans committee and hope to be a .member of the veterans committee next session. I spent a great many hours, time which perhaps I should have spent on my
Supply-Veterans Affairs

constituency, trying to solve these very matters.	I	appreciate	all that	has been	saidhere	by	hon. members, and	I know it hasbeen said in all earnestness and true sincerity ; but I wish hon. gentlemen would bear	in	mind the	fact that on this	committee there were sixty veterans of either the first or the second great war. I happen to be one of them. Please do give us time to work	out these	things.	We have	been
doing our best to work out these matters, and we shall do the same next year. But do give us a break, and do not spend all this time discussing these matters here, because all you are doing is detracting from the hard work the committee has done. We will give you everything we have at the next session, ' and I am sure many of these matters will be dealt with satisfactorily then.

As a veteran of the first great war I should like to make one observation. During the last war I corresponded with probably four hundred men overseas. AM those men, without exception, had one desire: "Get me a job; give me a job." Mention has been made of General Hoffmeister's remarks to the effect that a veteran ought not to have to dig ditches. I say this: Veterans want jobs. No one should make a promise to keep a man from digging a ditch if he is properly fitted for that work and if he digs a good ditch. I would much rather dig a ditch and be paid for it than be a white collar man and starve to death.
I make the plea to get these men back and give them work. Do not make too many promises, because these young boys become confused. My young brother-in-law enlisted at the age of eighteen and served six years with the flying corps. He is now twenty-five years of age, and upon returning home he does not know which course to take. My advice to him was: Get to work, and have the other fellow pay you while you are looking the ground over.
Give these men jobs. Those who are maimed or have become physically defective because of the war should be looked after one hundred per cent. Move them out of that disgraceful Christie street hospital, for which both Conservative and Liberal governments are responsible, and put them into a hospital we can be proud of. Look after the blind and the maimed. But do not promise those boys the world with a fence around it. They have served a great purpose. Do not fill them with promises. Give them jobs, and they will prove themselves worthy, as they did during the war. When they enlisted as volunteers they did not need promises to show what they could do. They do not want promises now,

with one exception, and that is that they have a job. Fulfil that promise of a job, so that they may do their work. They do not want to be keyed up with promises, take courses, and after getting half way through them, slip back and three or four months from now find their own levels. Give them jobs; and give those who are maimed the proper kind of treatment.

During the present session
there has been very little discussion of veterans affairs in the house. The main reason, of course, was that we had a special committee studying veterans affairs. I agree with other hon. members of that committee when they say it did good work, and I appreciated the privilege of serving on it. I believe every member who gave that service feels the same as I do, and I am sure we shall be able to do good work for the veterans in next session's committee.
The work of the special committee had to be limited to certain things; there was not time to cover everything. We recommended three bills which have now been passed by the house, one to amend The War Service Grants Act, another to amend The Veterans' Land Act and a third to provide rehabilitation allowances for veterans. That meant, of course, that we could not consider such vital questions as pensions, war veterans allowances and hospital treatment. It is true that some representations were made on those points, but there was no lengthy consideration of any of them by the committee. Now, of course there can be no further consideration until the next session.
The department submitted to the committee two draft bills, one proposing to amend the Pension Act and the other to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act. Those two bills show that departmental officials have in mind at the present time certain things in connection with those acts.
I have five questions I should like to ask the minister, which deal particularly with pensions and war veterans allowances. First of all, in respect of pensions, we have contended for a long time that a provision should be written into our Pension Act to the effect that a man's condition on admission to service shall be presumed to have been his actual condition, and that if subsequently there is any deterioration prior to his discharge, the onus shall be upon the state to show that such deterioration was not caused by his service. For some reason or other we have never been able to make much headway with that suggestion. The result out in the country where we meet the veterans is that

Supply-Veterans Affairs
time and again the pension commission holds that a man's condition was a preenlistment condition, and when they do that they may or or may not grant the applicant a partial pension on the ground that such preenlistment condition has been aggravated. But where the pension is based on an aggravated preenlistment condition it is always smaller than if it had been held that there was a straight disability.
I know of several cases where injustices have been done. These are not only men who served in Canada, but also men who served overseas.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
It does not apply to
overseas cases.

Oh, yes. I know of cases
where it has been found that a man's condition was a preenlistment condition, and he was allowed only an aggravation, and not an out-and-out disability pension. Sometimes I am tempted to blame the pension commission. If this goes on indefinitely there are going to be many veterans in Canada not receiving the pensions to which they are entitled.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In the event of aggravation of disability caused overseas, the applicant is entitled to the whole amount of the pension, unless the condition was obvious, recorded or wilfully concealed.

The difficulty is this. A man is accepted by the army, after many examinations. He is found to be perfectly fit. He goes overseas and in two or three years comes back, receiving his discharge as being medically unfit or in a lower category. Then, if you please, the pension commission finds that he had some preenlistment condition. In other words, although he was accepted as fit, and although everybody thought he was fit, several years later the pension commission decides there was something the matter with him when he enlisted and that therefore he is not entitled to full compensation for his disability. I know of cases where that has been done.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The principle of fit-for-service fit-for-pension has never been accepted by any country in the world.
I do not think the minister should emphasize so much Canada's having the best laws for veterans.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I was not referring to that.

I hope it is true, but I know that in some respects it is not. However that
is not the test. The test should1 be whether or not these laws could be improved, and here is an instance where they could be. I suggest there should be a section written into the Pension Act which will make the situation clear. I will suggest a section which the officials of the department and the minister might consider. It would read:
It shall he presumed-
And this is not something which takes place automatically; it is a presumption-
It shall be presumed that an applicant's condition as recorded on his admission to the service was in fact his condition at that time, .and that any subsequent deterioration was due to his service.
In other words this sets up a presumption in favour of the applicant.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is the same as the British provision?
Yes, it is practically the same as the provision in Great Britain.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My friend took this matter up last year in debate in this house. We made a thorough examination of the significance of the presumption which was embodied in the British amendment^. My advisers, rightly or wrongly, say that under the existing conditions the provisions under our Pension Act are more generous.
That is not the way the act works out with the disabled veteran. I know of cases in which the veteran is losing out.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We will study it between now and next session, and then it can be taken up by parliament.

If a presumption of that kind were followed by the pension commission it would mean that this man could qualify for a pension. Further I think the minister would find that such a section would change the outlook of his pension commissioners.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I shall be glad to go into it fully.

That is the first suggestion. It is important that the department should go into these matters before the next session. Do not let everything die now until the house meets again. It will be weeks later before the committee is set up and there will be no amending legislation until May, June, or perhaps even later.
My next suggestion has to do with the insurance principle. I am not going to go into this again, because the minister knows how we feel about it. We feel it should
Supply-Veterans Affairs

be restored to cover men who enlisted to fight, even though they were not able to get out of Canada. We do not want to protect the man who never had any intention of fighting, but these other men should be covered by the insurance principle. The minister has said that there has been a compromise section put in the act. He is quite right; that is section 11, subsection 3. It provides that if a man has been disabled and cannot qualify for a pension; if he is in difficult circumstances, then the pension commission may in their discretion award him whatever they feel like awarding. There is a means test to it, which of course is a bad feature. I notice in the submission of the National Council of Veterans' Associations, presented to the special committee this year, it was pointed out that not only is there a means test at the start before the man qualifies for a pension, but the commission can go back and back and means test the man. If his financial condition improves, his pension may be reduced or taken away altogether. They suggest that once a man qualifies he should be entitled to have his pension continue.
Then there is another serious difficulty. Under that section a man may have a pension granted by the pension commission-* the minister will correct me if I am wrong- but he never gets the full amount according to his disability. Even though a man is 100 per cent disabled he can never get more than two-thirds of the total disability allowance under that section. That is so, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That may be correct; there was a feeling that there should be some distinction made between that type of case and the battle casualty overseas.

That needs to be given further consideration. If a man is 100 per cent disabled and is entitled to pension under this section, he should get a pension corresponding to the amount of his disability. I would ask that further consideration be given to that. Then with regard to war veterans allowances, which have been mentioned briefly today; this act is to be changed as well. By the way, the changes that I have mentioned were not included in the draft bills the minister handed to the special committee this year, and that is why I am mentioning them here.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is no such thing as a draft bill before this house.

It was before the committee. The amendments that I am going to suggest to the War Veterans Allowance Act were not in the bill the minister put before the committee either. I think eventually the means

test will have to be done away with under the War Veterans Allowance Act. The dominion government has proposed to the provinces that old age pensions will be paid at seventy years without a means test. The war veterans allowance was supposed to be a form of old age pension to the veteran who had been burned1 out. He was made eligible for allowance at sixty years of age instead of seventy. If the principle of automatic payment is put into the old age pension legislation, I think it will have to follow into the war veterans allowance legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We are trying to be mutually helpful in regard to the pension situation. Out of over 40,000 pensions payment, more than 5,000 were awarded for service in Canada only.

I think if the minister
checked up on the other figures covering the applications for pension he would find that the percentage of those who can get over the hurdle in Canada is very small, unless it has jumped a lot since last year. There should be a widening of the right to earn without disqualifying one for a war veteran's allowance. The man *who has been thrifty all through his life and put away a little savings cannot get a war veteran's allowance until he has spent practically all of his savings. He cannot have a proper home in the city without losing a portion of his war veteran's allowance. The restrictions are too severe and I suggest that they be studied carefully before the committee meets again.
The minister took a surprising stand this morning with regard to imperials. It is an old argument, it is a poor argument, but it sounds good. The minister said that we cannot allow any imperial to get a. war veteran's allowance because there were thousands of Canadians who got to England1 but who are not eligible for war veterans' allowances unless they are pensioners; therefore why should anything be given to imperials? That sounded different from the speech made yesterday by his leader on the question of indemnities. There may be two wrongs here, but it is no answer to one to say that there is another wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will go this far with my hon. friend: cure the first one first, cure the Canadian one first.

The qualification for a war veteran's allowance is based on service in a theatre of war, and the only request that has ever been made by an imperial for a war veteran's allowance was by an imperial who had served in a theatre of war.

- Supply-Veterans Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is quite correct.

That should not be confused with the Canadian who did not serve in a theatre of war. If the minister is correct in his stand, the Canadian who never served in a theatre of war would get a war veteran's allowance before the imperial who had served in a theatre of war.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The request made to us by the association was with reference to imperials who had come to this country up to 1930; it was asked that they be entitled to the benefits of the veterans' allowances. That would mean that the Canadian who had served in England would'not have preference over the ex-imperial who came here in 1930.

The minister is taking the two groups together, the one group who actually served under fire and the other group who did not. I think that is an unfair position to take. I am not trying to deprecate the claim of the Canadian who only got to England, but certainly that does not meet the situation of the imperial who was under fire and who came to Canada after the last war. That man gave up rights under the social security measures in Great Britain which were far greater than anything he would receive here. He became a Canadian citizen and has stood shoulder to shoulder with us ever since that time. He cannot qualify now simply because of an argument such as the minister has put up to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am afraid I am being annoying, but may I say. this to my hon. friend, that I know of no Canadian parlia-ment-I am not speaking about parties or governments-that has yet accepted responsibility except for Canadians who left the shores of Canada.

There were domiciled Canadians, men who left the shores of Canada some years before the fighting took place. I do not agree with the minister. He has gone this far, and I am glad to get him out in the open. When we get' into power we shall meet, the problem of these imperials; if I have anything to do with it, we certainly will.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I 'hope they do not have to wait that long.

It may not be as long as the minister thinks. He is just whistling to keep his courage up.
Another question on which I should like some assurance has to do with what we call the non-pensioned widows. They are now
entitled to a payment; what they really get is a war veteran's allowance, and they are getting that payment under an order in council. It- has never been put in statutory form.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is that not in the new bill my hon. friend has in front of him?
The minister said a few moments ago that this is not a bill. Is it or is it not? I agree that it is in this hypothetical bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is to be considered by the committee.
Is there any doubt that they are covered by the order in council in the meantime? That order in council will not be invalid in the meantime because of the termination of the War Measures Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They are covered this year by the appropriation act, and will thereafter be by the proposed measure to be considered by the select committee when it meets again.
I*suggest that the minister give consideration to putting it in statutory form if there is any doubt about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We have given that definite consideration, and we have no doubt whatever about their being covered.	t

My final question has to do with the dual service pension. It is called a pension, but is really a war veteran's allowance. The submission has been made that the payment should be on the basis of a reward for service, in other words, a service pension for long service to the country. Most of these men were three or four years in the first great war and perhaps five years in the second. It is only fair that the payment should be based on that service rather than on a means test. I have no doubt that the department considered that aspect of it, but can the minister explain why it was not made an actual pension rather than a war veteran's allowance?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Because the request was definitely received from some of the leading veterans' organizations to have it considered not as a pension but rather as an allowance under the veterans' allowance act. I say with the utmost frankness that it is not a success as it is now, and I think it should be one of the duties of the committee next session to go into the matter thoroughly and make new recommendations in regard to it. I do not think that the dual service order is any good.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
I hope that the minister and his able officers will work out some suggestions for the committee by, the time we meet next year.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We shall do that.
I agree that it is a difficult question, but I suggest that the payment should be based on service rather than on a means test.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We shall be glad to consider that. I think we have had a very fine ' debate, Mr. Chairman, and I wonder if I might now ask the committee to make some progress with these estimates.

Mr. Chairman: I must protest at the rushing through of important business at this time. This is the only opportunity the members have of getting the ministers before them to deal with matters of the kind, matters about which all members receive letters, telegrams and other communications with which we are bound to deal. Let us remember that we are now receiving overtime, and there is no reason why we should not work for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think we are.

So far as I am concerned I am going to deal with these matters now.
I have never taken up the time of the house in dealing with veterans' affairs. It was not necessary for me to do it because the veterans have exceedingly capable representatives in this house wrho have been doing a good job for the veterans ever since I have been here.
Someone suggested this afternoon that we take a realistic view of this question. It was the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Case) when he was referring to the point made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) that when veterans are unable to secure employment they should be given an adequate living allowance. I think we have established that principle too, and I do not see why the veterans should not have the benefit of it as well as members of parliament.
It was realized some time ago that the question what would happen to men of the armed services when they return fro it) overseas was a very live one. It was an important question in the federal election campaign in May and June of this year, and all candidates took a considerable part of their time to deal with it. In everything that I had to say on this question, either at public meetings or in broadcasts, I made the point that so far as legislation was concerned Canada had good legislation for the returned men-perhaps, as the minister has said, the best legislation in

the world. I think that is conceded. But I pointed out that if economic conditions in this country became depressed, no matter what special provision we had made for the veterans, the veterans nevertheless would suffer. Economic conditions now are becoming depressed, and a veteran who .would not have difficulty under prosperous economic conditions will find himself in difficult circumstances as economic conditions become worse, and he will come to the government for relief. So the question that is confronting us to-day is not simply a question of dealing with legislation for the veteran; it is a question of dealing with the whole economy of Canada and the committee requires considerably more time with the Department of Labour, the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Department of Reconstruction, perhaps the Department of Agriculture, and the Department of Finance. All of these are interwoven and will have to coordinate their efforts before we can successfully cope with the problem of improving economic conditions. I put myself on record as supporting the proposal made by he member for Cape Breton South that the veterans should be granted an adequate living allowance if employment cannot be found for them.
I1 have another matter to bring to the attention of the minister and I bring it up because I promised to do it. The corps of Canadian fire fighters overseas has sent a brief to the minister which perhaps was discussed at the veterans committee. The gist of the brief is that these men should be given the same benefits as the men of the armed services. I asked some questions in regard to the number of Canadian fire fighters who went to the United Kingdom from Canada, the average length of service, and how many were killed, wounded or died of serious injuries or illness overseas. The answer was that 408 went overseas; the average length of service was two years, eight months and fourteen days; three were killed, five wounded, and five seriously injured.
Obviously these men were a part of the fighting forces. Is there any reason, therefore, particularly considering that the number is so small, why they should not be given all the benefits accruing to other returned veterans? Of twenty-two enlistment benefits for veterans, six benefits have been received; five benefits have been received with conditions attached, and to eleven benefits they have no entitlement at all.
I suggest to the minister that he put the fire fighting corps on the same basis, so far as benefits are concerned, as the men of the other armed services.

Supply-Veterans Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I thank my hon.
friend for his remarks. Whether we were right or wrong, last year, when we passed the order in council, a distinction was made by the committee, on advice from various departments that there should be a differentiation between those who were members of the armed forces and those who were not; therefore it will be found that supervisors and some of the ancillary services, such as fire fighters, do not receive the entire amount of benefits that are received by members of the services. Whether that was right or wrong is a question I shall not debate now, but that was the dominant argument behind the decision made at that time. As a matter of fact, I remember very well receiving a delegation from the fire fighters in my office when the projected order in council was under discussion, and they appeared at that time to be satisfied with it, although since then there have been marked complaints. The whole question will come up before the committee of the house next March.

I want to help the minister get through as quickly as possible; therefore I shall be brief. I know that he is one of the hardest working ministers of the crown; far be it from me, then, to detain him longer than is absolutely necessary. In the first place, I feel it my duty to compliment the minister on his programme, in reference to making the recommendations or regulations, or whatever they are called, having to do with non-pensionable widows, into a bill and making them statutory.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think my hon. friend deserves most of the credit for that.

No. The minister deserves the credit, and I will give him all of it. I was just a humble worker following his programme. The minister really did a great service to the country, because non-pensionable widows were a part of the population who had not got a fair deal. The minister tackled the problem, and I happened to help him, and in due course these widows were looked after. I am glad to see that the matter will now be made statutory.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The vote is increased
by SI00,000 this year.

I am glad to hear the
minister say that, and again I compliment him. I wish to say a word with reference to fire fighters. The chairman is very humble and modest. He could have taken a great deal of credit for the fact that the chief of the fire fighters overseas came from his own fine city of Brantford. I am right in that, 47696-225|
am I not? Yes, I am. A large number of these men came from Toronto, many from my own riding, but like many other members I have risen to bring up the problem of these men. I am not competent to say whether their work was comparable with the work of the soldiers, but a number of them were killed and others were wounded, as we have heard to-day. For my part I am satisfied to leave the matter in the hands of the minister. If he can do anything to give these men fair play I know he will.
I wish to bring up a couple of cases I have mentioned before, and again I am going to be brief. I want to be as kindly as I can, and therefore I begin by saying that personally I have always had the utmost courtesy and satisfaction from the minister and his staff. I have no complaints to make in reference to the way I have been treated. However, I was greatly concerned in reading, as other members have been in the last few days, about the shooting of Canadian soldiers overseas, as strikingly recorded in this morning's Globe and Mail of Toronto in the following article:
Lonely Walk of Canadians to Death Told. By Ralph Allen, staff correspondent of the Olobe and Mail. Aurich, December 14.-A story of sadism and mental torture that sounded like an oriental horror tale entered the records of the Kurt Meyer trial to-day as one of Meyer's former soldiers described how a German officer stood in a monastery courtyard and hurled taunts .at seven Canadian prisoners of war just before he sent them through a little ivied gateway, one at a time, to be shot dead by .an SS corporal waiting for them on the other side.
That article recalls to my mind the case I brought up before of George Stevens, who lives on Salem avenue, Toronto, and whose number is 57727. What I fear is that Mr. Stevens, perhaps in bitter resentment of the fact that he has been unable to present his case so that it will be sympathetically heard, has written to the department letters which on being read were not at all favourably received. I do not blame Mr. Stevens, because he was-a prisoner of the same type about whom L have just read. He and others were captured' in a trench in Belgium and lined up against, the wall. He understood a bit of German,. and he heard the officer in charge of their captors saying, "We will shoot these English-ers." He called them all English, using that word. Just at that moment a German officer came along and, on being told what was about to take place, prevented the shooting. I can well imagine the horrible feeling that must have possessed these Canadian prisoners on being lined up to be shot.
I fear that the gentlemen of the department who have to do with such oases do not
Supply-Veterans Affairs

quite realize the effect which this has had on these men. I know Mr. Stevens very well. I have known him ever since the war ended. On many occasions I have seen him sitting on the edge of the sidewalk, helpless, unable to move. But when he is taken to hospital and put in a nice clean comfortable bed, with nurses to wait on him, after he has been there a day or two the doctors take his temperature and they pronounce him one hundred per cent fit. That does not sound to me like common sense. If I wanted to get the truth about such a man I would oall in his neighbours. They are the people who see him daily. They meet him here, there and everywhere, and I would take their word in preference to the word of a staff of doctors from here to Jericho, because the doctors see him only after he has rested and his blood pressure and nervous energy have been restored. I brought this case up before. The minister kindly said that he would look into it and he did. I know that, but he took the reports from his staff. Forget all about the staff.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I cannot afford to do that.
That is the unfortunate part of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They are very efficient.

That is what I say; they are honest and qualified. They get their reports from the doctors in the hospital who see the man after he has been there two or three days and has regained calm equilibrium. That is not the right basis to go on. I know a man whose condition was brought to the attention of the department. I did my best to get some consideration for him." I was told by the commission that he had no case, but he died. The man knew he was right, but the doctors thought they were right because they examined him after he was in the hospital for some time and had become shiDshape.
I had another case brought to my attention the other day, that of Francis J. Rider, whose number is 465004. I have known Mr. Rider for twenty-five years. He used to be an employee of mine. I have seen him in all sorts of conditions. I have gone to his house and found him hardly able to breathe, with froth running out of his mouth and down over his breast. He is making a claim for bronchitis, which he claims he contracted due to his war service, and I believe it. I knew him before he went overseas. He was placed in the hospital and the doctors saw him a day or two after he was there. But it was after he had been attended by pleasant nurses,

waited on, his meals brought to him three times a day. Naturally he regained a calm equilibrium, his breathing became all right and the doctors looked him over and pronounced him a hundred per cent. That does not mean very much to me.
I know of another case, a Scotsman, in whom I believe. He would not need to swear on a bible for me to believe him. I have seen him in an abject condition. His name is William Robertson, and his number is 534262. I took up his case- with the department, and I really believe the department has tried to do something for Mr. Robertson. They made an investigation; they sent him to Christie street, and recently they sent him to Ste. Anne's. I have seen him in a pitiable condition many times in his own home, but when he gets into these fine warm beds with pretty nurses waiting on him, serving him meals three times a day, he makes a great improvement. Then the doctors come in, look him over and pronounce him a hundred per cent. I am going to leave that with the minister. I ask him not to take the medical report but to take the report of the neighbours on the street who have seen this man in the condition which I have 'described. If the minister does that, and I trust- him, he will give these three returned soldiers a square deal.

I should like to add my voice to that of the hon. member for Vancouver East. I prepared a long brief on this matter, and I agree with the hon. member when he says that he does not think sufficient time is given to these important problems. I am not going to threaten the minister with a forty minute speech, and what I say may be a little disjointed because it is difficult to boil down a forty minute speech into a five minute one.
Something should be added to the argument made on behalf of these fire fighters. They should) be treated as ordinary veterans are treated. At the end of niy five minute speech I know the minister is going to tell me that the committee is giving this matter earnest consideration and that he is quite sure that something will be done about it next year. But he has not stated definitely that a bill is to be brought down to put these men on an equal basis with the veterans. I presume at this stage the minister could not promise that in so many words.
In fairness to the Canadian fire fighters I say that in view of the conditions of their service and the terms of their employment they should be granted all the rights and privileges which have been granted to the

Supply-Veterans Affairs
military forces. In reply to the hon. member for Vancouver East the minister said that the differentiation is a matter of combat service.
I should like to give from memory the words of the Minister of National Defence when he said very heatedly that so far as he was concerned the front lines were where the bombs were falling, irrespective of whether it was in England! or on the continent. I am in full agreement with him there. These men were subject to military discipline and' military pay. They suffered the risks of the actual veterans, and in some cases more risks, because they helped defend England! at an important time in her history, when bombs were dropping on all sides. Evidence of that is given in the fact that several of them were killed.
I am not going into a long argument as to the benefits which have been denied these men. One of the most important, at least to the young men, is the denial of the right to have an education at the expense of the people of this country. These men are not all seasoned firemen coming back to their jobs. Some of them are young boys who left school to go into the fire fighting forces. I have a letter or two from several of them who complain that they cannot now complete their education. One or two of them have taken on liabilities in the form of wives, and they would like to get some further education, but they cannot do that. I shall read one short paragraph from one of the letters:
In addition to the disappointment of every member of the corps, the omissions of this order in council have very far-reaching effects for me personally. I was married overseas, but due to the uncertainty of the available financial aid, my wife will not be able to join me until next spring. Prior to enlistment, I was a student at the university of Saskatchewan where I was enrolled in a type D arts course leading to theology. I am planning to return to university this next term, but am keenly disappointed that I shall have no financial assistance in the form of an educational grant. It may mean that now, with family responsibilities, I shall he unable to complete my chosen course.
These men have almost everything in common with the regular combat soldiers. They volunteered for the duration of the war; they offered life and limb. Like any other soldier, they accepted discipline. They accepted comparable pay and allowances; their term was like that of the soldiers. The carried Canadian army cards, and were medically checked and finger-printed by the Canadian army. Their conditions of eating and travelling and so forth were the same. I would say to all intents and purposes these men were simply Canadian soldiers who were defending Britain, iust as the first division may have been said
to be defending Britain all the time it was over there even though it' had never fired a shot.
I believe the main argument which is motivating the government-I am not speaking for the government-is that there has to be a line drawn somewhere. I am guessing again when I say that the government may say that if we give it to these men, a great many other auxiliary services will say, "If they get it, we should get it," and so on. I think I have answered the argument that these men are not military personnel. I have shown that they carried different weapons, weapons of defence; that they suffered the hazards and the conditions of the war. They were subjected' to the risks of fire and' of war, of falling bombs.
I have shown how they accepted pay and discipline comparable to that of the army.
The government may argue that to meet this demand might precipitate demands from other services. I do not think that argument is valid. These men were more nearly on a par with the military than with any of the other serivces, as I have shown. It is true, and I think this is a good argument, that these men did not receive as high a rate of pay as some of the other services; that is to say, they were restricted simply to military pay. It will be said, of course, that we cannot afford it. I am not going into that matter at the moment, but when millions of dollars are being voted here every day, the cost of meeting the claim of these men would be a mere drop in the bucket. You may say I am becoming financially as irresponsible as a [DOT]Social Crediter, and that may be so. Personally I am not worrying very much about the national debt; so far as Britain is concerned, for instance, I do not think as yet she has paid back the money she borrowed to beat Napoleon in 1815, and I do not suppose our debt will be treated any differently.
There is just one other point I should mention. These men were never promised the full rehabilitation grants, but time and again they have said they understood they would receive them. I am not going to delay the committee longer, but I promised I would bring up this matter and I have done so to the best of my ability. I thought probably the minister would prefer to have me spend five minutes on it now than forty minutes when the item concerning fire fighters came up.

speechtext: At the moment I cannot make a definite declaration of policy, except to say that the Pension Act will be reviewed by a committee of this house, probably some time next March, and any complaints made by hon. members will receive sympathetic consideration at that time.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
404- Veterans' bureau, $224,137.

In the submission to the special committee by the National Council of Veterans' Associations in Canada there was a recommendation that the veterans bureau should be an independent commission having authority and freedom equivalent to that enjoyed by the Canadian pension commission. Then they went on to suggest that the chief pensions advocate should have powers suitable to his office and equal to those of the chairman of the pension commission. They further suggested that the office of travelling inspector of the veterans' bureau be filled by a full-time advocate, in order that he might exercise constant supervision over the work of preparing cases in the district offices of the bureau. I-think the minister will agree that there always has been a feeling that because a pensions advocate was paid by the government he might not be working 100 per1 cent for the soldier. I am not saying that has been the case, but there always has been that reaction, so it does seem to me this suggestion is worthy of very serious consideration. Brucellosis is the United States term for Bang's disease or contagious abortion.
Regarding the immediate reduction of losses, which with questionable accuracy is eometitmes designated "control," our results fully support the original claim that the vaccine provides valuable protection. Despite failures, which we should learn to expect even when fresh live vaccine is used, the vaccination prevents, delays or mitigates a high percentage of brucellosis.
At the bureau's animal disease station, Mingle and Manthei have conducted experiments in. which they have proved that under conditions which should favour such a change, it has been impossible to increase the virulence of strain 19. They have also shown that when strain 19 is injected intravenously into pregnant cows in such large doses as to cause abortion the infection disappears before the next pregnancy, and that if normal pregnant cows have contact with them and are exposed to aborted fetuses, they fail to become infected.
In addition to these two experiments that were conducted under most exacting research procedures there are many other reports of work of a similar nature, and probably hundreds of instances in which calves have been vaccinated in negative herds without spreading infection to other animals. Indications are, therefore, that there is no danger of strain 19 reverting to an onanism of increased virulence or that, in its present degree of stability, it oan establish disease in vaccinated animals or spread disease to
associating animals. So far as we know there is
not a single ease on record at present in which .infection with strain 19 has occurred through contact with vaccinated animals.
That is the general opinion in this country, and that is probably why strain 19 has not been accepted here as it is in the United
States.
Haring has mentioned several herds in which brucellosis has been controlled by whole-herd vaccination with the subsequent vaccination of calves. It appears, therefore, that whole-herd vaccination will have beneficial results in infected herds in suppressing infection and abortion.
In our control programme adult vaccination must obviously be restricted. We must not lose sight of the fact, however, that much more good than harm will .result from whole-herd vaccination, that it is the most simple plan to adopt to inhibit the spread of infection and abortion, and. therefore, that it is better than a do-nothing policy.
Whole herd vaccination, with subsequent calf vaccination, in herds of the kind indicated, is a matter that justifies serious consideration by state officials. The bureau recognizes the fact that whole-herd vaccination is being performed in many states of the union without the sanction of the state authorities and in many instances in violation of state regulations. To permit the dhe.of vaccine in .animals other than calves, the restriction on labels of vaccine containers will be modified in the near future. It is believed that if .adequate information can be made available on the advantages and disadvantages of adult vaccination to owners of infected herds it will result in closer cooperation between herd owners and regulatory^ officials, and will result in the suppression of infection and abortion in thousands of herds that would otherwise be untouchable so far as supervisory control is concerned.
It is our aim to eliminate brucellosis from our cattle population. To safeguard the progress we have made in the federal-state programme and to extend our services in this connection, we should make use of 'all methods available. Particularly should we concentrate on practices within the economy of time and man-power that will accomplish greatest results and of a kind that will adapt themselves to the post-war or normal continuation of this work.
Why is it then that there is a law in this country against the use of strain 19 for whole-herd vaccination? I have shown that in the United States they have proven satisfactory results can be achieved both in the case of calfhood vaccination and in whole-herd vaccination where the outbreak is of a serious nature.
It is my belief that this disease, commonly known as contagious abortion, has probably caused to cattle producers the greatest loss of any disease affecting cattle in this country. True, as the minister said the other day, a great many listed herds are annually tested free of charge by veterinary inspectors of the health of animals branch. It is, however, my sincere belief that these listed herds are by
Supply-Agriculture

far the mo^t vulnerable, having neither natural nor acquired immunity; and as long as the disease is present in the community or area, these listed herds are most susceptible to a severe outbreak of the disease, because it is practically impossible to protect them against infection by any or all of the accepted principles of sanitation.
It is true that strain 19 is not a cure for the disease, but used wisely it can be of great value as a protection against its occurrence. It is my belief that calfhood vaccination should be part of the listed herd plan. Otherwise we are only developing a herd which will tend to defeat the purpose, as evidenced by the number of outbreaks in listed herds across the country in the last couple of years.
Whole-herd vaccination should be legalized for accredited veterinarians, to be used only in the case of severe outbreaks of the disease. As was pointed out by my colleague, the hon. member for Lanark, this disease not only affects cattle, but causes a condition known as undulant fever in humans, making it doubly important that every possible method be adopted to inhibit or prevent its occurrence. But with the present staff in the health of animals branch it is practically impossible to carry on any further programme. Therefore, in order to do anything in this regard we must get the men first. Salary increases should be brought about in order to get men. We should then go on and complete the present tuberculosis eradication plan. Would the minister kindly consider recommending the vaccination of all calves to be raided in the listed herds? Whole-herd1 vaccination by accredited veterinarians in the case of severe outbreaks should be also recommended, and when an adequate staff is available we should follow in the accredited areas with a plan to vaccinate all calves to be raised, such as they have carried out in the state of Connecticut.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I was not clear whether the hon. member had in mind that in the department we were still following the practice that we followed up until about two years ago when we did not recommend1 the use of calfhood vaccination at all. As a matter of fact we recommended against it. I forget when our policy was changed, but during the last couple of years we have been encouraging the use of calf vaccination in this country.
In the discussion that I had with the hon. member for Lanark the other night I think I said that we were giving consideration to the application of somewhat the same principles to the treatment of Bang's disease as we have followed in the past in connection with tuber-

culosis. I hope to be able to discuss it at greater length next session when we bring down the estimates for next year, but at the moment our chief problem in connection with all these matters is the one which was raised by the hon. member for Brant at the beginning of what he had to say, namely, staffs to do the work. It is not altogether a matter of pay, although I admit that if we had higher pay or higher inducements to men to come into the veterinary profession a few years ago we would have more of them to-day. Up until about the time the war started our chief difficulty was that there was so little in live stock, because of the prices that were being paid at that time, that veterinarians were seldom called. As a result of their not being called they simply disappeared from the countryside. We have a great many of the veterinarians that could be found across the country working for the government, at the present time. Many of them just had to leave the country districts. They were not able to make a living. That is probably the chief reason why there were not more men to take a veterinary course. Therefore our difficulty to-day is to find veterinary surgeons in many parts of Canada who have had considerable experience. For example, where I farm I have to go thirty-five miles to find a veterinarian.^ It takes a pretty good animal to pay a man to come thirty-five miles even in good times. In poor times most people just do the best they can in treating the animals and do not call in a veterinarian. That situation has changed to some extent, and it makes it a little more difficult for us. Men are called to-day and some are inclined to go out and establish their own practice in certain areas. On the other hand, we are trying to' get back some of the men that we had before the war. Some of them are now coming back.
Some comparison was made between the numbers we had in certain places before the war and the numbers we have had within the last year. That is somewhat due to the fact that we have been at war. Many of them enlisted in some branch of the war services, and some of them are now coming back. So that we are gradually getting these men back into the service.
The other evening we discussed the question of the salaries of these men and the salaries of other technical men. At that time my, hon. friend was not here, but I suggested that in the Department of Agriculture we had perhaps gone farther under the order in council which was passed last April, in having special cases checked and reclassified, than any other department. But we know we have not gone far enough, and we are all looking for-

Supply-Agriculture
ward to a general reexamination of the staff now that the war is over, bringing together the allowances which were paid in lieu of cost of living during the war and the salaries listed in these votes, in order to improve the position of many officials of the department. I have no doubt that as time goes on, and without too much delay, many of the difficulties that have been complained about will be removed.
I would offer only one criticism with regard to the comparisons made in the early remarks of the hon. member, when he mentioned the Department of Munitions and Supply and the different war services. I think it is obvious that salaries in those branches would have to be better. To a certain extent they are temporary; people have to be induced to serve for short periods of time. The comparisons made by the civil service commission, and made by ourselves when we are checking, are rather with the established departments that continue right on through the years, whether we have war or not, and that will be with us all the time. I do not know whether we are on all fours with all other departments, but as I said in discussing the main estimates it is the job of the civil service commission to see that we are. I think we raise the question ourselves as often as any department in the service, and each time it is argued that our men are paid on the same basis as those of any other department. It is difficult to answer an argument of that kind put up by a commission which has been established by this house and which has authority to make these decisions. However, at all times we are working for a better standard of pay, although we have to take into consideration salaries paid in other departments and other services.
As between this country and the United States there are many reasons why at the present time it is difficult to keep our pay at the same rates as theirs. . Their price standards and wage standards are out of line with ours all the way through, but whether they have a greater value than ours is another question. One would have to go much farther than just to compare salaries in order to arrive at a conclusion as to whether the lower rate of pay here carries with it the same purchasing power as the higher rate of pay in the United States. Just to quote the dollars does not give the whole answer, although I admit that salaries for this kind of service are and have been for some time much higher in the United States than in this country, and I agree that many of our good men leave Canada and go to the United States on that account.

In the case of part-time
veterinarians the pay now is S10 a day- for a maximum of fifteen days a month. Does the minister find difficulty in obtaining veterinarians at this rate?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I could not say that we have had difficulty in getting them. On occasions men have said that they did not want to take on departmental work, because they had sufficient work of their own, but usually we have been able to get the part-time men who are available across the country at the rates we have been paying. I would hot argue that they are paid enough.

I asked that question
because if there had been a heavy outbreak of cholera in western and southern Ontario counties last fall, I wondered whether men would have been available to look after it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
In what I have to say with regard to these estimates I hope I may be both brief and constructive. In the first place, as a new member of the house I have been surprised' at the meagre amount of time that* has been devoted to the highly important subjects of health and welfare, although we have been sitting here for over three months. I believe there are reasons for that. Perhaps the house has foregone a discussion of these questions because the dominion-provincial conference has been in session. Those of us who sit in this part of the house have refrained from doing anything to muddy the waters of delicate negotiations between the dominion and the provinces. I believe the government will realize that we have deliberately refrained from doing anything to embarrass in any way the progress of negotiations, because there is no field in the whole realm of government in Canada in which it more vitally important that there be the closest possible cooperation between dominion and provincial governments than in the kindred 
fields of health and public welfare. One can only hope that whatever recommendations may come out of the dominion-provincial conference, or whatever its decisions may be, it will be possible to bring about closer cooperation in order that health and welfare measures may be forwarded to the general advantage of Canada. The health of all the citizens of Canada is and must be the concern of all the citizens of Canada, and similarly in regard to measures of necessary social security.
One matter of regret I have is that, in the framework of committee organization existing at the present time, there is not any provision for a standing committee on health, welfare and social security. For some years there has been an informal committee Which meets at the call of the minister or the chairman. The committee consists of representatives fiom this house and the other place, but it has no official status and I believe, has met on only three occasions during the present session.
If I am not mistaken, the minister himself might welcome action on the part of the house toward setting up a permanent standing committee in the fields of health, welfare and social security. I can conceive that it would be of infinite advantage to the minister if there were such a standing committee. That would be the committee to which questions could be referred for close and detailed study which, unfortunately, the house when assembled either as a house or as a committee of the whole just cannot give.
The country is moving forward in these matters, and if there ever was a time when it was desirable that the committee structure of the House of Commons should be revised and brought up to date, surely that 'time has come. There is much in the committee organization that is archaic. Here is one situation where the need of a newly constituted standing committee has been abundantly proven.
For these reasons I hope the minister will forward, during the time between this session and the next, proposals for a revision of the rules of the house to provide for the appointment of a standing committee on health, welfare and social security. I would urge, further, that in the interval between this session and the next, the government should also give consideration to the inclusion within the scope of the Department of National Health and Welfare a subject which in my humble submission really belongs to that department. In Great. Britain the subject of housing, and the responsibility for the administration of government housing policies, is vested in the ministry of health. At the present time in Canada under the present organization, much

Supply-Health and Welfare
of the housing policy is administered by the Minister of Finance. To some extent there has been intrusion in this field by the minister of Reconstruction and Supply. The Minister of Finance is greatly overworked, and his department is a heavy one. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has recently shown his readiness to take on additional responsibilities while the house has been in session. There has been assigned to him general supervision over the national film board, and also over Canadian information service, the successor to the wartime information board. It may be that if given an opportunity the minister might be prepared to assume responsibility for supervision of the housing policy in 'this country, and I think such administration might logically be placed in the department which he heads.
I wish just to offer this concluding suggestion, that in the administration of his department, the minister should at all times endeavour to the utmost to use the existing social services provided by the provinces in the administration of whatever social measures are embarked upon by the federal government. There is no field in which it is more important that there be some attempt at unified administration; and with qualified bodies already in existence and trained to deal with social problems, I suggest that they should be used in the administration of whatever social measures are inaugurated by the federal authority.
The last thing we would want to encourage in Canada would be a multiplication of social and welfare services doing parallel work. It. is very much better in these matters relating to health and welfare if we come down as close as possible to the people who are in need of the services; and the governments in closest contact with those needs are the municipal and provincial governments. I hope that the policy followed by this department will be one of trying to use existing srevices provided by provincial govenments, or under provincial legislation, and 'that there will not be any considerable amount of unnecessary duplication of services, a condition which can result only in wastefulness and chaos.	.

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
May I say just a word in acknowledgment of the helpful suggestions made by the hon. member for Eglinton, and also by other hon. members who took part in the discussion of these estimates on December 3. We appreciate their encouraging and helpful suggestions, and I can assure all of them that their suggestions will receive the most serious consideration.
To-day the hon. member for Eglinton has referred to the importance of dominion-provincial cooperation. I can assure him that we have that very much in mind. As I said earlier, we were happy to be able to report that we have the closest of good relations with all provincial departments of health, their ministers and officers. I believe the committee would be interested to learn that, following the meeting of premiers who constituted the coordinating committee of the dominion-provincial conference, an economic committee on dominion-provincial relations was set. dp, and that I had the honour of presiding over it. We held meetings from December 4, and ad-"ourned yesterday until January 8.
During the course of those meetings the health and welfare officers of the provinces came here, and we had some very useful discussions. I have been authorized by the conference to state that the discussions which dealt with the clarification and development of the dominion proposals, and matters arising from them, were carried on in a most cooperative spirit, and that substantial progress was made.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I should like to say a word about the shortage of nurses in Canada, although the training of nurses is a subject which comes more properly in the provincial -Id. However, if we are to go into the subject of health services we shall require many trained nurses. Many civilian hospitals do not train nurses, with the result that there
a marked scarcity. At the present time the government is disbanding young girls from the three services, but there has not been offered to them any special training along the line of nursing, into which vocation they could be readily absorbed.
I suggest that grants could be made to civilian hospitals and provincial hospitals by the government, to remedy this shortage. At the present time people are going to hospitals because they cannot obtain nursing . services at home, or nurses who will take private duty. I know it is almost. impossible at times to obtain nurses for people who are ill, and this shortage prevails both outside the hospitals and on. hospital staffs. Has the minister any intention of .making grants to public hospitals to facilitate the training of nurses in view of the fact that we are considering a programme of health services?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
That question was raised when the estimates were up before, on December 3. At that time I gave an account of the relations between the department and the Canadian nurses' association, and mentioned the grants made by the government to that

Supply-Health and Welfare
association to stimulate the recruitment and training of nurses during the war, at a time when a shortage had been created because of war conditions and the heavy demand by the armed forces and the Department of Veterans Affairs. I said at that time that it was not the present intention of the federal government to continue this assistance into peace time. We do not consider we would be justified in continuing this assistance any more than we would be justified in granting assistance for the training of doctors, dentists or any other professional group for which there was a need in Canada but which ordinarily come completely within the jurisdiction of the provinces. I may add that we have not had any suggestion from any province that such a grant be given and that there have been discussions at which such a request would have been made had it been in the minds of the provinces to make it. At the present time I can only tell my hon. friend that it is not the intention of the government to make such grants, either for nurses or doctors, because that is regarded as a provincial responsibility.
