maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Has the government anj plans for the extension of hospitalization facilities or services in the dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The proposals of the Dominion of Canada made to the provinces, which will be found at page 36 of the green book, provide for loans of money at cost or slightly over cost to the provinces or through the provinces to municipalities and other authorities for the provision of hospitals. That is the only proposal made so far. In addition, we have our own responsibilities with regard to the hospitalization of members of the armed forces, veterans, Indians, sick mariners, quarantine and the like, which come within federal jurisdiction. This proposal has been made and is now under consideration by the provinces.	.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Following up the minister's reply, I take it that there is no thought on the part of the federal government of launching into a programme of free hospitalization in the country.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The proposals put before the conference include a nation-wide system of health insurance which would provide complete free hospitalization for every Canadian man, woman and child in every part of Canada. The details of this will be found on page 31 of the green book; the proposals are 
spelled out there. They provide for a basic grant by the federal government of one-fifth of the estimated cost of the services that are shown in the table and an additional one-half of the actual cost as shown in the table, within the limits set out in the table. Those costs are to be revised every three years. The federal contribution would be roughly, 60 per cent of the cost of providing these services. The services may be inaugurated by the provinces in stages, either with regard to the different services or with regard to different areas. They are very flexible and are designed to meet the criticism of the health bill that was made before the social security committee of the House of Commons which met in 1943 and 1944. These proposals are now under active consideration by the provinces; if they were accepted, after a term of years we would have a system of free hospitalization for every Canadian in every part of Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
It would be impossible to provide the benefits under any such scheme as the minister describes because of the shortage of hospital beds in Canada. There is a shortage in the case of general hospitals and in the case of hospitals for the chronically ill. There is a shortage of beds everywhere and there are whole areas without accommodation. There are whole provinces without convalescent hospitals; in fact I believe there are only two in Canada. There is a definite shortage of tuburculosis sanataria and a shortage of mental hospitals. I believe that in Ontario there is something like 5,000 waiting cases. One might say the present number of beds in use. is 101,000 and the total present need is 143,000; the total estimated need in Canada in ten years is 161,000. Apart from these types of hospitals, there are only fifteen isolation hospitals in Canada. Is it the purpose of the minister to increase the grants for the building of hospitals in order to meet this shortage?
Mr, CLAXTON: The proposals made by the dominion government are designed to put the provinces in a position where they can _ discharge their responsibilities. No doubt the provinces in considering these proposals will have in mind the need of additional capital equipment, including hospitals, and they will make up their minds whether the proposals are adequate or not. What my hon. friend says about the shortage of hospital beds is quite true. We know his interest in this subject, both because of his profession and his interest in public health, and the facts are just as he states them. This matter is dealt

Supply-Health and Welfare
with at length in the reference book on health, welfare and labour which was placed before the conference. At page 31 and following will be found elaborate tables dealing with hospital accommodation and needs in Canada.
The health insurance plan could not be introduced at once even if the provinces agreed and we passed the necessary legislation to bring it into effect on January 1, 1946. This would not be possible for a number of reasons. First, we would not have the necessary hospital accommodation, neither would we have the doctors and neither would the doctors be in the right places. Another reason is that we would not have the administrative experience and skills necessary to introduce the plan all at once on a nationwide basis. From discussions with experts in this field one reaches the conclusion that if we go forward along the lines of this programme the best we could possibly hope to achieve, is to have it in operation in four or five years. I know that most provinces are planning to do a good deal of hospital construction during that period just as soon as materials and labour become available.
In this connection I should say that we aim to have in the department a consultant architect on hospitals. The position has been advertised, and it brings with it a good salary so that we hope to attract a very high type of architect and equip him with a knowledge of hospital construction and planning throughout the world. He would be available to consult with the provinces, the municipalities and the local agencies. He would not draw the plans, because their own architects would do that, but he could offer skilled consultant services and submit typical plans, specifications and the like. We hope to supply that service, and it is being done to meet a resolution passed by the dominion council of health.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The other question arising out of the minister's answer had to do with the medical care being provided by the minister's department for returned veterans and their families. I . am particularly interested in the care given by the doctor of the veteran or the family, and I should like to know what is the relationship of the services that are being administered by the department in that respect.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: As I understand the hon. member's question, he is referring to medical care given to veterans under the order in council that was passed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The minister referred to
the obligation of his department in the matter
of providing medical services to veterans and their families. I am concerned with the relationship of that service to the normal relationship that these people would have with their own doctors.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I was referring to the
jurisdiction of the federal government. The hospitalization provided by the Department of National Health and Welfare has nothing to do with hospitalization or treatment given to veterans and their families. That is a matter for the Department of Veterans Affairs except that the Department of National Health and Welfare has to do with the furnishing of emergency services, inspection and the like, of veterans' families in transit back to Canada. That is done thrpugh. the ordinary immigration medical service and quarantine service.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: May I ask how it is proposed to achieve a common standard of treatment throughout the various provinces? Some provinces are much ahead of others in matters of public health. Saskatchewan has been doing a great deal in T.B. for years. Will there be some liaison between the provinces and will the federal Department of Health exercise some supervision to achieve a common standard for the whole country?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
That will remain to be
worked out with the provinces if an agreement is arrived at. The draft bill which was attached to the report of the committee of the house on social security in 1944 provided for an advisory council at the federal level and for committees' in each province which would work out just the kind of thing my hon. friend has in mind. We have had a good deal of discussion over this, and I consider that it would be relatively easy to work out, in cooperation, common standards and objectives. It is recognized, however, that we could not all go at the same pace. The needs of some of the provinces are quite different from those of other provinces and it would be necessary to institute certain services in some of the provinces to fill urgent needs, where other provinces already have such services and they would do something else. But the objective would be to achieve a nation-wide high standard of medical services for everyone within the shortest possible time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
What is being done in the
matter of research, and what is set aside for research in maternal mortality, infant mortality, and such diseases as arthritis, infantile paralysis, cancer and tuberculosis, which are extremely important?

Supply-Health and Welfare

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The national research
council is charged with responsibility for research in Canada, and medical research has been largely carried on under its auspices. It has a medical committee and a number of subcommittees which operate in different fields. A considerable amount of research has been done, largely by universities, hospitals, institutes and the like, with assistance from the national research council. The federal department of pensions and national health, as it was until last year, now the Department of National Health and Welfare, has not engaged in: any extensive medical research. It is carrying on some research in various fields, such as nutrition, development of standards, public health, epidemiology and so forth, but not in medicine.
With regard to cancer research in Canada there is, as hon. members know, the King George V Silver Jubilee cancer fund which was raised in 1935 and amounts to approximately $500,000. In the years from 1937 to 1940. $14,000 was paid out of that fund each year to the cancer committee of the Canadian Medical Association. In 1940 it was agreed with the association that half of the grant would be paid by the association to the Canadian society for control of cancer. In 1942 the grant to the association was reduced to $7,000 which was turned over directly to the Canadian society for control of cancer, this reduction being made at the request of the association, which found it difficult to continue its educational work among the medical profession during war time. In May, 1945, at the request of the association the full amount of the grant was reinstated for this year, to be paid to the Canadian society for control of cancer, covering expanded activities of the society. We have just recently asked the cancer committee of the Canadian Medical Association to discuss with us plans whereby the whole fund, capital and interest, will be used for cancer research, and we hope to have very shortly something started in that direction.
Cancer research is being carried on in England and the United States on a very large scale, and if we are to do anything effective in cancer research in Canada we would have to do it on a pretty large scale. We do not want to duplicate the work that is already being done in other countries, and it will be necessary to coordinate our work with theirs and make the most effective use we can of the money. The payments made to the cancer committee of the Canadian Medical Association were used by it largely

for education and information, bringing it home to people that they should take early steps to secure a diagnosis of cancer and treatment at the earliest possible day.
With regard to arthritis, I do not know of any work being done under the auspices of the national research council. With regard to maternal and child mortality, I would have to make inquiries to find out what research work was being done in those fields, if any.
As my hon. friend knows, research in Canada has been carried on very largely in institutes like the Banting institute, the Connaught laboratories, McGill university and other universities and hospitals. It has not been regarded up to now as a function of the federal government and not very much as a function of the provincial governments. We are reviewing that whole position; we are endeavouring to cooperate closely with the national research council and we hope to work out a policy which will coordinate all these activities and see that anything that should be done is done.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: When the house reassembles at eight o'clock I shall be asking a short question about, the splendid work being carried on in Toronto under the auspices of Doctor Hincks. Perhaps the minister would refresh his memory and give the house some information on that after eight o'clock?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I should like to ask a question with regard to cancer clinics and what arrangements are made with the provinces. Is there some standing arrangement whereby the federal government will contribute on a fifty-fifty basis in raising the standard of health in a province which is prepared to take advantage of assistance of that kind? speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
If health insurance comes into effect, then cancer will be one of the conditions dealt with by hospitals administered under the provinces, and so would arthritis. They would be treated like any other condition, and there would be no need for special provision or assistance.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I should like to mention the mental hygiene programme presided oyer by Doctor Hincks, of Toronto. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
National health branch-
195. Quarantine and leprosy, $187,647.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Would the minister give an account of the work carried on in the leper hospitals in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am glad to say that the situation regarding leprosy in Canada is one of continuous improvement. As the hon. member for Lanark knows, there is not a great number of lepers in Canada. At the present time there are two leper hospitals for the treatment of leprosy, one at Bentinck island, British Columbia, where, I am glad to say, there are only two patients; one is Chinese and the other, Japanese. Both cases are bacteriologically negative. We have another hospital at Tracadde, New Brunswick, where there are seven patients, of whom three are of French-Acadian origin, one of French and Scottish descent, two of Russian ancestry, and one, Chinese. There is no part of Canada where leprosy occurs among Canadians except
in that particular neighbourhood of New Brunswick, and I am glad to say that it seems to be almost completely arrested. The operations of those two very small hospitals do not cost very much. Treatment is given, and we hope that before very long it will only be necessary to keep these hospitals to take care of any case of leprosy that should turn up on ships coming to the country.

speechtext:

Mr. MacIN'NIS:	This is an important
subject. I note that the -estimate has been reduced by $14,000 since last year. It was not a large one last year, considering the importance of the work. Will the minister explain the reduction?	.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: This amount is given to the division of maternal and infant hygiene to make available the distribution of literature and information on this subject. I am not sure of the actual reason for the decline. It does not mean that there will be any interruption or reduction in the amount of the work in this field. I should like to point out that there is a supplementary estimate of $47,584 under this head. That is the explanation I was seeking when the Minister af Justice pointed it out to me. That has enabled us to extend the work. I think most hon. members are familiar with the work of Doctor Couture. His book on "The Canadian Mother and Child" has probably had a greater circulation than any other book in Canada with the exception of the bible, and it must have contributed considerably to the substantial reduction in the maternal and infant mortality rates which have occurred since 1926. Since 1926 the reduction is almost fifty _ per cent, which shows that substantial progress is being made.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I have been impressed with the very good pre-natal care that the doctors are now giving, and also the post-natal advice which the young mothers get. In addition to the baby book, is any other work being done? The quality of the services has increased so much I suspect that the department is cooperating with the doctors in supplying the information.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Yes, that is quite true. The results that have been achieved in the reduction of maternal and infant mortality have been due very largely to the information supplied, to the development of clinics and to the much greater percentage of mothers who receive pre-natal attention of one kind or another. The interesting thing, and in some

Supply-Health and Welfare
way perhaps a most unfortunate thing, is that the improvement is reflected to a far greater extent in the cities than in the country districts. Our hope would be that with the institution of anything like a nation-wide system of health insurance, the benefits which now can be obtained in the cities by the mother for herself and her child, would be extended to the whole population. During the war a greater percentage of births took place in cities than previously, and that has largely contributed to the marked improvement in these figures. But while I say there' is a marked improvement, Canada still is not registering nearly'as high a record in these fields as she should, having regard to her high standard of living, and we hope to work with the provinces and other agencies to bring about a steady improvement.

National health branch-
ZOO. Treatment of sick mariners, $329,488.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
For a moment I should
like to discuss a matter connected with this item. I do not think the minister can do anything about it just now, but I hope he will give it some consideration between now and the opening of the next session. The fund for sick mariners and marine hospitals is provided for in section 305 of part V of the Canada Shipping Act, and is raised in two ways. In the first place, there is a levy on ships entering Canadian ports, and to the extent that this does not pay for the service given, the remainder comes out of the consolidated revenue fund. I have not the figures with me; perhaps the minister has, but I am not going to ask him to look into that matter. This year it was drawn to my attention that ships plying between ports in the same province did not pay into this fund and that consequently employees on such ships were not entitled to these benefits. For instance, a ship on the Pacific coast plying between Prince Rupert and Vancouver does not pay into the fund. Neither does a ship plying between Victoria and Vancouver, but a ship going from Vancouver to Seattle does pay into it, and so does a ship crossing the strait from Prince Edward Island to New Brunswick.
I had prepared a bill to rectify this omission from the shipping act and to bring all ships under the same provision, so that all would pay dues and all crews would be eligible for the benefits of the fund. I found that such a bill would not be in order, since it would impose a tax and, could be introduced only by a member of the cabinet. I should like to ask the Minister of National Health and

Welfare if between now and the next session of parliament he would look into this matter with a view to amending this section in order to meet the condition I have mentioned. I had quite a discussion on the matter with the Minister of Transport, who, I, thought at first, would have control over it, but later on we found that he did not. I should like the minister's assurance that he will look into this, because I think such an amendment is desirable and would be quite equitable. I do not think I need say more, because I know there is nothing he can do now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I think I am right in
saying that the only vessels which are exempt from the requirement that they should pay into this fund are those engaged in the coasting trade within one province.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: And between Ontario and' Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
So that it is a matter of provincial jurisdiction. The 'other vessels, even though they may be engaged in the coasting trade, contribute on the basis of two cents per flat rate ton, I think, the same as ocean-going vessels. Whether or not additional vessels trading wholly within a certain province should be included would be a matter for discussion with the provinces.
This service is really extraordinary in extent. It provides emergency treatment and' hospitalization for a period of up to a year.. During the period under review the service actually treated 18,316 sick mariners. During the time Halifax was probably the greatest port in the world we had a boat of our own which would go through the convoys. If any ship in a convoy wanted the doctor to call, it would hoist the appropriate signal and our doctor would go aboard and give whatever treatment was required. In addition to that, sometimes we dealt with as many as three and four thousand cases each month in Halifax alone. The service was widely used and greatly appreciated. I shall be glad to discuss with the Minister of Transport the representation of the hon. member.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I believe that a number of hon. members are keenly interested in the medical investigations being made by some people in connection with arthritis. From what we' have heard I believe that the minister has most humane qualities and that he would not overlook this matter. I would plead with him to give it his attention.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Perhaps I should make it clear that, in our concept, research into medical conditions in Canada can best be conducted by hospitals and by institutes actively operating in those fields. It has never been
part of the federal function to do that research. However, the medical committee of the national research council has assisted in research projects along various lines. So far, we have not undertaken any of these matters ourselves, but it has been the policy of the government to coordinate all research under the national research council. As I said before the dinner recess, we are actively discussing with the national research council the possibilities of greater coordination and development. The hon. member's representations will certainly be considered.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
National health branch-
201. Industrial hygiene, $8,665.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What is the relationship between this vote and the provincial departments of industrial hygiene? We have really only one official, who operates in this matter. What does he do? What does the medical officer do under the industrial hygiene vote?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
To a great extent the industrial hygiene division of the department has to do with the improvement of standards of health in war industries, in consequence of actual contractual obligations they incurred with the federal government to do such work. Our officers work very closely with provincial government officers in trying to improve industrial hygiene standards in war plants, and also in some other plants that are federal in character.
Gradually we have transferred to some of the provinces both the laboratories and the staff. I have in mind particularly British Columbia where that has been accomplished. However, we have worked closely not only with the provinces but with the medical officers of the major corporations engaged in the field of industry. I believe that the results achieved were good. We hope that in consequence of this work, the work will be continued under provincial auspices. It is our desire to keep a small division operating, to cooperate with the provinces, but not nearly to the same extent as was done during the war.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will the department have anything to do with medical industrial work in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If there is any industrial problem we certainly would be very glad to deal with it. However, so far as I know we have had no occasion to do so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That would be undei federal authority, would it not?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Yes, we have a division which would be equipped to deal with a condition of that kind, if such arose.

Supply-Health and Welfare

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
At this late stage of proceedings many of the most important items have to be glossed over on account of lack of time; and when one rises to speak he feels almost that he is guilty of wrongdoing. However, I rise at this time to suggest that the department might be well advised to take note of the medical investigations which have been carried out for some years by the United States in the Aleutian islands. It will take only a minute to tell the committee about this most important work. In 1911 a treaty was signed between the United States and various countries, including Canada, to protect the seals on the Pribyloff island. Following that year the' United States took charge of the island and established there a colony or village. The colony consisted of Aleuts, as they are known, who are a group of people of Russian extraction.
Since those years following the establishment of the colony the United States has sent medical men, dentists and nurses each year. It was my privilege only a few months ago to hear Doctor Sexton in a private interview relate what had been discovered. I believe that the discoveries are well worthy of investigation by the medical men in the Department of National Health and Welfare. It was found that as soon as the natives of the Aleutian islands ate the same kind of food as we were eating they lost their teeth, with the result that there is not an Aleut on the island today of twenty years of age or under who has his teeth. Their forefathers who ate fish and blubber, who never had milk or any kind of vegetables, had fairly white teeth, until they changed their diet.
The United States sent medical investigators, including some dentists. For a number of years they have been investigating conditions among the natives, with a view to learning the cause of their losing their teeth. It has been discovered that there is a certain element in food which is closely related to sunlight, and which in fact is one of the vitamins. Vitamins are now being put into the food, and experiments are being conducted to see if they cannot at least preserve the children's teeth.
These experiments are of such a nature and of such importance that I suggest our medical officers would be well advised to find out what the Americans have discovered through the years. Here is a group of people who were not in touch with so-called civilization and who, since they have been supplied with food by that civilization, have lost their teeth. It is most important that we find out the causes.

I have been told that those who are conducting the investigations are going to be up against the dentists, because they think they have discovered why the natives have lost their teeth. It is pointed out that the dentists do not want to have the inquiries conducted any further.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
It would interfere with
private enterprise.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I lost my teeth-and
not through private enterprise.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
In some countries the state,
not private enterprise, looks after teeth. I believe that the department would be interested in this matter of the restoration or preservation of teeth.
It will be noted that Doctor Stefansson, one of our own medical men, has been conducting experiments along the same lines, and he has discovered that the Eskimos, who never tasted food as we understand it, and who have never had milk or vegetables, had good teeth.
I believe that this matter is serious enough to warrant our cooperating with the Americans who are making these investigations, learning the facts from them and, whether we tread on the toes of any of the professions, making that information public and available, so that, if possible, we may preserve the teeth of our children.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
What study has been made
in connection with cancer? I believe this has been referred to by other hon. members. I am not quite sure what the nutrition service embraces, but perhaps the minister would give us some information about this disease.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
This nutrition service has provided the people of Canada since 1941 with information about sound nutritional practices. This is a small vote, as hon. members will see, but a great deal pf work has been done, largely through the officers of the department working with local committees, local health officers and provincial officers. From time to time campaigns of education have been organized, and general promotional activities have been carried on to create interest in nutrition. I think it is within the knowledge of everyone that during the war, despite the shortages which existed, the nutritional habits of the Canadian people improved almost out of recognition, just as they did in England and in some other countries. We have distributed hundreds of thousands of posters and pamphlets and carried on all kinds of educational activities, all of which have borne fruit. This is primarily a promotional and educational activity, but in addition some research work is being done in

Supply-Health and Welfare
conjunction with other government departments and other agencies and we hope that there will be some constructive results.
I should like to make just one observation on the comments of the hon. member for New Westminster with regard to diet. Mr. Stefansson, to whom he referred, used to be a Canadian. He had considerable experience in the far north, and in an article in the current number of the Atlantic Monthly he refers to the absence of caries in the mouths of people who live on a meat diet. However, he points out that it takes about seven pounds of meat a day to feed those people.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The thing that has attracted my attention is the small amount of this vote. It appears to me that the. Department of National Health and Welfare should recognize some responsibility in establishing high national standards of industrial hygiene. I am thinking of the mining industry where silicosis is fairly common. I understand that the governments in the different provinces have passed certain regulations with regard to this, but in some cases they are not lived up to. I thought one of the functions of this department might be to carry on inspection work to see that high standards of national industrial hygiene are lived up to.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: We have no jurisdiction.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Could not one of the functions of the department be that of pointing out to provincial governments whether or not their standards are being lived up to?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I do not know whether the hon. member has gone into this extensively, but I would think the provinces would consider that they were up to the job of dealing with their own functions in this field. The dominion council of health has on it representatives from the different provinces, and perhaps that body could bring the matter to their attention and secure their support for some concerted action. I think that would be the right way to proceed, but as a federal government we certainly could not set standards for the provinces to follow in the field in which they have exclusive jurisdiction. All we can do is to help with and supplement the work they are doing and meet the needs as they express them to us. As a department we have not done anything with regard to silicosis, but the national research council has carried on certain work. Major Blaisdell, in conjunction with the province of Ontario and Lake Shore mine and certain other industries, has carried on a good deal of work in this
field, but that is a matter which is regarded as falling within the field of the workmen's compensation board of each province.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The health records
of the different provinces show that there is a need for greater enforcement of health measures in factories and industry. To-day we are dealing more and more with chemical production; we are carrying on more spray painting, and our factory production generally has increased a great deal. There may be no place constitutionally for us to go to a province and tell them that they are not living up to certain standards, but I think a branch such as this could point out that the standards are very low in some provinces and assist those provinces to raise them. The department could act more in an advisory capacity than try to enforce something. I understand that there are limitations, but it would be a nice thing to be able to say that, in Canada there are certain high standards which we are trying to maintain.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I can only repeat that if we tried to step into provincial fields and told the provinces what they should do in matters of health, then the kind of cooperative activities that we want to carry on with them would be seriously jeopardized. We can get the provinces to sit down and discuss things in which we have a common interest, but I for one would not subscribe to any policy by which this government would dictate to the provinces what the standards should be. They have been dealing with industrial standards and the like for a great number of years; they have very good health departments, and while they may have varying standards, they also have varying needs. More and more they are working together and consulting with each other. We are very happy to work with them to do what we can to supplement their own work, but it is certainly no part of the role of this department to trespass on the proper functions of the provincial governments.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am only advocating cooperation, not coercion. I think the standards are pretty low.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The question of silicosis comes up periodically. Silicosis is an industrial disease which can be elminated completely. Doctor Robson and the late Mr. James Denny of the Mclntyre-Porcupine mine have developed an aluminum therapy treatment which has proven to be a major step in the right direction. I understand that a foundation has been set up largely supported by the Mclntyre-Porcupine mine and other mines

Supply-Health and Welfare
in the district, as well as some in the Kirkland lake area. At one time silicosis was a problem in this industry, but with proper precautions and the use of aluminum therapy it can be completely eradicated. This is one of the great things that has been done by Canadian medicine in the last ten or fifteen years.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
National health .branch-
203. Nutrition service, $69,027.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Everything the department is doing in the way of promoting better [DOT]nutritional standards is well done; the money that is being voted is money well spent. The minister has said that the efforts of his department in this direction are bearing fruit, but I thought the purpose was rather to promote consumption of fruit.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
National health branch-
. %0-!(. Combating venereal disease-administration, $24,678.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: This and the next two items have to do with measures to combat venereal diseases. Would the minister make a statement as to the progress being made in combating this dread disease. In particular, I would ask him to say something concerning the cooperative basis on which the dominion and the provinces are uniting their efforts in this field. I think the new approach to this problem is commendable in so far as it urges a frank and realistic approach and insistence on sound standards of education. At the same time I am bound to say that I do not approve furthering the cause by subsidizing attacks on religion, which is the foundation of all morals.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I was going to ask the same question.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
For a number of years the federal government did give a considerable amount of assistance to the provinces, which was discontinued for some years and then was resumed in 1943. A venereal disease control division was established in the former department of pensions and national health, which was taken over by the new department. One of the first things I had to do as minister of the new department in October, 1944, was to approve a series of advertisements as part of a nation-wide campaign to develop interest in and1 direct constructive attention to this important subject. Hon. members will recall that this series of advertisements emphasized the four-sector front against V.D.-health, welfare, legal and moral. That was a four-

pronged attack on this subject which was developed by this department. While the frankness of the advertisements and radio publicity and the motion pictures that were shown from one end of Canada to the other might have been alarming to some people, there was not a word of criticism of them from 'any quarter. The result undoubtedly was a much more frank discussion of the whole subject and a much stronger attack on it from all sides.
During the war there has been close cooperation between the armed services and the provincial and local authorities controlling the disease. That was made possible through our having seconded to this department or its predecessor Colonel Williams, who was V.D. control officer of the army. With him came other officers from the armed forces, and we were fortunate in being able to establish with all the provinces the closest kind1 of cooperation. One of the developments in that field which was interesting and new was the reporting of contacts, and a great deal of useful work was done there. The result in figures is indicated in the report of the department, which shows that in the armed forces, the only branch of the population for which there are any really reliable statistics, there was a considerable decrease in the incidence of syphilis, particularly between 1940 and 1944, whereas one might have expected that there would be an increase. The problem is receiving continuous attention, and the department's division will continue to cooperate in the way in which it has been doing with the provinces and municipalities in this field.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

speechtext: This is a service that covers the whole nation. Will the minister outline the way in which his organization is set up across Canada, and at the same time indicate what measure of cooperation there is with the provinces and to what extent, if any, departments of provincial governments are used in the administration of this service?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
With regard to the administrative set-up of family allowances, I should say we endeavoured from the start to have the most complete decentralization. Registrations were made at the office established by the family allowance administration in the capital of each province; from that office the payments are made, and with that office correspondence is ordinarily held. The extent of this can be readily understood when 1 inform hon. members-I hope it will surprise them-that we have engaged in the family allowance administration at Ottawa only seven persons, the rest of the work being done in the nine offices established in the provincial capitals.
Cooperation with the provinces takes several forms. In the first place, we have made an arrangement with every province whereby we
Supply-Health and Welfare

provide a recordak equipment and train staff to make microfilm photographs of the records of births and deaths of children under sixteen. That work is well advanced, and the films are sent to Ottawa where information from them is put on cards by the dominion bureau of statistics. From these card registers are produced containing a list of the children in each province, by years. That index is sent to our provincial office and applications for family allowances are checked against it. In that way we have obviated the necessity of requiring individual applicants for family allowances to provide evidence of the birth and existence of children.
Second, the Family Allowances Act, as hon. members know, provides that the children in respect of whom allowances shall be paid shall be children who are attending school, and we have construed that to mean attending school in accordance with the provisions in force in each province. In every province we have received the most whole-hearted cooperation in the enforcement of that provision.
I can tell of one case recently brought to my attention where the regional director of family allowances told me that in a certain district in a province where ordinarily only about ten per cent of the children went to school in September, this year it is ninety-five per cent. The provinces have not only cooperated wholeheartedly in this respect, but they have been exceedingly glad to do so because it has, generally speaking, reinforced their own provisions with regard to school attendance.
The third respect in which we have had cooperation from the provinces is in ensuring that the allowances are properly spent. We
do not propose to police the spending by investigating every home, but we hope to work out, either with the provinces or with agencies in each province, or by other means, arrangements whereby we shall have close cooperation in this direction. We have had conferences with child welfare organizations, children's aid societies and the like, and from those conferences we are gradually constructing the framework for relations with the provinces which we hope will secure complete cooperation in this respect.

I just wish to congratulate the minister and the officials of his department on the commendable way in which family allowances have been administered. When family allowances were first suggested many people said that it would result in the establishment of a, bureaucracy. From every point in my constituency I have heard nothing but praise and commendation for the administration of this act.
I just wish to draw to the attention of the minister one case in my riding which I think should receive sympathetic consideration. It is that of a young girl who is within the age limit to receive the allowance. She is quite normal but suffers from a nervous affliction which requires her to attend a school in the United States, in Washington, I believe. It is the only school of its type in the western states. There is no school of the kind in Canada. Because this child has to go to that school and be absent from Canada over a certain period her parents are denied the allowance. I do wish the minister would give some consideration to cases of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

Could the minister give us some details of the item of $150,000 for publicity and information, and $150,000 for professional and special services? These items are to be found on page 137 of the estimates.
Mr. CLAX'l'ON: With regard to the item for publicity and information, it will be readily understood by hon. members that one cannot deal with all the people of Canada, which virtually we are doing in family allowances, without a considerable amount of expenditure on information. We had to expend quite a large sum in order to secure the registration that was made in the form in which it was made. Had we not spent so much we would have spent more on clerical staff to secure corrections. The money paid in family allowances payments is good in itself, both from the point of view of both the children and the family, and the economy of the country, but we consider that it is not enough just to pay this money out. We should like to do what we can to develop interest on the part of the parents to spend it in the best possible way for the benefit of their children. Therefore, from time to time, in conjunction with provincial and .local authorities, we intend to develop interest in various matters relating to the health and welfare of children. We believe that money spent in that way will

Supply-Health and Welfare
prevent the necessity of so much money being spent in policing. We therefore put in this considerable amount with the thought that it would be spent on films, exhibits, and in various other promotional activities, to draw to the attention of Canadian parents the possibilities of spending the money in the best interests of their children.

In dealing with social and welfare agencies an item has come to my attention which I think the minister really appreciates, since through me he has obtained some knowledge of it. I should now like to bring it to the attention of the committee. A Canadian soldier overseas married a British war widow who was the mother of children. In this particular instance the woman is the mother of three children born to a British father. She is now the mother of two children by the Canadian soldier. They are now living in my home city of Owen Sound. While the Family Allowances Act has made provision for the two children born of the Canadian father, who is still in the armed services overseas, it makes no provision for the three children born of the British father. As I have said before, the family allowances are intended for the welfare of the children of this nation. We hope to make them better citizens and give them greater opportunities than heretofore. While the act makes no provision for a case of this kind, I feel that it should be amended. I would urge the minister and his department to give serious consideration to that, because there must be many more similar cases where widows overseas with children born to a former marriage have married Canadian soldiers and have come to make their home in Canada. Some of them are now mothers of children born to Canadian soldiers, but there is no provision
for the children of the first marriage. I am not going to say that these children are wards of Canada, but they will be future citizens of Canada. I would therefore urge the minister to give serious consideration to changing the act so that these children may be included.

speechtext:
I understood that we could discuss on the civil estimates any war appropriation estimate. I do not know whether the minister is proposing to call the old age pension item or not. I believe that now comes under his department although it is listed as being under the Minister of Finance. I have no intention this evening of dealing with the question of an increase in old age pensions or the lowering of the age limit, because those points were discussed earlier in the session. However, I should like to ask the minister whether his department is taking any steps to bring about a change in the regulations under the Old Age Pensions Act. I realize that the questions of an increased pension and the lowering of the age limit are being deferred until the conclusion of the dominion-provincial conference, but there is no reason why some steps should not be taken in the meantime to bring about a change in the regulations.
It takes time to do these things, and in the case of our older citizens, time means so much. They have to be seventy years of age to come under this act, and when one gets along to that age, every day counts. It is a tragedy that there has been such a long delay in getting these provisions through. The present 47696-227J
regulations are too harsh; I think the minister will agree with me on that. The result is that in Canada many of these people are not able to establish their eligibility for pension. If the minister will refer to page 37 of the Dominion of Canada proposals made to the dominion-provincial conference he will see it is stated that only about forty per cent of all persons of seventy years of age and over are able to establish eligibility for old age pension. Doctor Marsh in his report of two years ago- and I refer the minister to page 70-states that in Great Britain about eighty per cent of the people over seventy years of age are able to qualify, either for old age pensions or similar assistance. He goes on to point out why there is this difference and traces the cause right back to the harshness of the regulations. This harshness is also dealt with in the proposals made by the dominion government to which I have referred; the minister will find this at page 38. The dominion is now proposing that for the ages sixty-five to sixty-nine there shall be a joint plan, the dominion paying half and the provinces paying half; it is admitted on page 38 that certain changes will be necessary, designed to liberalize the conditions under which the assistance is given.
Further down on the same page it is proposed that residence in Canada should be required only for a period of twenty years since the age of eighteen, including a period of three years immediately preceding the date of application for a pension. That, of course, is far more liberal than the present regulation.
It is also proposed that the maximum payment be reduced by the amount of the applicant's personal income, if any, in excess of $125 per annum, but the submission goes on to say:
In computing the income of the recipient for purposes of this means-test, moneys received from other sources not for the recipient's own use to be excluded. The pension would only be reduced to the extent that the pensioner had outside sources of personal income for his or her own use.
I presume that would mean that there would not be such drastic restrictions as there are at the present time for example, that pensioners might be allowed to own their homes without having a reduction made in the pension on that account. It goes on to say:
The existing requirement that payments made by way of old age pension must be recovered where possible from the estate of the recipient *after his death would be abolished.
These proposals are contained in the dominion government's own brief. The minister is aware, by the way, that Doctor Marsh goes into much greater detail. Is there any
Sup-ply-Health and Welfare

reason why steps could not be taken now to work out an easing of the regulations? It will have to be done sooner or later. It is only a matter of delay and that delay will work a hardship on many of these older people. I suggest to the minister that one of the most useful undertakings which his department could handle now would be to bring about a revision of the regulations to ease their restrictiveness.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: 1 should like to make this comment with regard to the observation of the hon. member for Vancouver South that only forty per cent of Canadians who are within the age group qualify for pension on the means-test, while the percentage is very much higher in Britain. That might mean a greater stringency of regulations or it might mean that there is a very much higher average of savings on the part of the people of this country, or a higher degree of independence.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The minister knows that the findings of Doctor Marsh are along the same line.

No regulation by reference to which any agreement with a province has been made shall be altered except with the consent of such province or in accordance with the provisions of the regulations to which it has agreed.
So that any alteration of the regulations can only be made by agreement with the provinces. I am very glad to tell the hon. member, however, that we have already inaugurated discussions with the provinces alongside the work of the dominion-provincial conference, and their welfare officers have accepted our suggestion t/hat early in the new year we should meet together to discuss administrative problems relative to old age pensions. We hope at that time to remedy some of the difficulties to which the hon. member has referred.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is very good. In view of the nature of the act the lead has to come from the dominion and I am very glad that that lead is being given.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
This is one branch of the department which I believe can do a great work for Canada, particularly if the films to be sent out of Canada in exchange for the

films of other countries cover Canada from ocean to ocean and from the international boundary to the Arctic. There is no other country in the world that can rival Canada's scenery and resources all along the line. I am not going to delay the committee to talk about them because it is too late in the session. I hope that at another session this vote will come down early so that members from every part of Canada can tell of the wonders of their own part of the country, not only the natural wonders and its resources but also Canadian industries, all of which could be portrayed to the great advantage of Canada, as well as everything that enters into industry in this country by way of productive employment. I wish to register my strong support for this particular branch, and I hope that when reconstruction is under consideration the minister will persuade the Minister of Public Works, under whose department I presume it would come, to put up a modem up-to-date building to house this branch. I was in the film building, if it is still the same one, in which the records are kept, but what is required to-day is a steel and concrete fireproof building to contain and preserve these priceless films that have been taken of Canada from one end to the other.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am not going into detail at this stage. I have in the past been extremely critical of the national film board on account of their documentaries and the propaganda they contained, but I have not seen one in the last year, so that I am not going to say anything about them. What are the new functions of the national film board? Are they to make films, for instance, to assist the immigration department by showing life in Canada, so that people who wish to come here may have an idea of what life here is really like? Are documentaries to be provided for showing in other countries to attract tourists to Canada? It seems to me there is a tremendous opportunity in the film board to show Canada abroad in a way that no other media can do.
I said, Mr. Chairman, that if the national film board is going to undertake the production of major films as well as documentaries we should have more information as to what the board proposes to do. I suggest that if you are considering the production of films of major length it would be wiser for us to know what the policy is. Are you going to compete with the private producer of films, or are you going to cooperate with the commercial studios? And is it the intention of the national film board to establish, or is it thought possible to establish a moving-picture industry in

Supply-Health and Welfare
Canada? If you are going to produce commercial films-and I hope you are not-then I suggest that you might consider the filming of "The White Tower", if the rights have not already been sold. That would afford us a wonderful opportunity to show our national parks in such a film, and Mount Assiniboine would suit very well as the locale for such a picture. Would the minister tell us what the forward policy of the film board is? I have had the report, but it does not say specifically.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
If this supplementary estimate and the amount that is voted in the estimates are expended this year by the national film board the cost to the people of the country will be $1,145,965. That is a large amount of money, and the question I ask myself is:	Is this expenditure worth
while? The question I ask the minister is: Does he think this expenditure is worth while? Does the board play an important part in the lives of the people of this country? Does it play an important part in the lives of members of parliament? It plays no part in my life, and I do not think it plays much part in the lives of most of the members of this assembly. So far as I know it plays no part, or if it does it plays only a small part, in the lives of the people of my constituency. I doubt if the government can carry on a film business anj' better than it could carry on a weekly newspaper. I suggest, therefore, that the whole matter should be very carefully looked into before further expenditures are made. I understand that recently the Royal Canadian Air Force asked the national film board to make a film for its women's division dealing with hygiene, that the national film board made that film and charged the R.C.A.F. over $20,000 for it, and that when the R.C.A.F. got the film they were so dissatisfied with it that they refused to use it, although they had to pay the bill. They, therefore, went to a private concern in Montreal and got them to make a film which they found satisfactory and which cost them much less. Can the minister tell us something about the film prepared by the national film board for the R.C.A.F., whether or not it was used by the R.C.A.F., whether or not the R.C.A.F, refused to use it and afterwards got a film that was satisfactory from a private concern in Montreal.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
When I spoke I had in mind films sent outside Canada, not those shown within the country. On one of my last trips to the United States I saw some of these Canadian films shown there, and from what I saw I took it that the intention was to
show our American cousins the marvellous tourist attractions we have, and to business people there the opportunities for investing money in Canada. I was not thinking of films shown here but of what it says, international, or outside the country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I would say this about the national film board. I think it is more than an organization; it has now become an institution and one which I wish to see perpetuated and enlarged. The national film board has brought great credit to Canada outside this country and has been of great service to Canada within it. One hon. member asked, does it play an important part in our lives? I think it does, and I am speaking for our group when I say that it plays an important part in the rural areas of western Canada. It is an invaluable source of adult education, and from that point of view alone we should like to see it continued and, indeed, expanded. The hon. member said that it played no part in his life. I suggest to him respectfully that that is his own fault. It has played quite a large part in my life.
I have gone frequently to the film board headquarters and rented films at the very reasonable rate of twenty-five cents a roll on all subjects under the sun, and have shown them in my constituency to all sorts of people. The board has a great part to play in this country, and I should like the minister to spare a few minutes to tell us what the future policy envisages for it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Davenport spoke of the desirability of our using films to spread knowledge of Canada abroad, a work in which he himself has been engaged for a great number of years. I venture to say that no agency of the Canadian government has done more to spread knowledge of Canada abroad as the film board. In the year under review it produced a total of 308 films, and I would ask hon. members who are interested in the subject to compare that production, from the point of view both of quality and of quantity, with the production of any other country on the face of the earth. If they do so they will find that we are second to none in any regard1.
The national film board has come to have a reputation abroad which puts us virtually second to none in the documentary fieLd. I have had the honour of representing Canada in some international conferences, for example, of UNRRA and the international labour organization, and at all these the national film board is there showing films to the representatives of other nations-films of Canada
Supply-Health and Welfare

and films of their own countries which our film board is aceumulating-and knows how to show. On more than one occasion the national film board has been chosen as the agency, the sole agency, of the international authority itself, as being the best in the whole worldi to do the job. The national film board was engaged by UNNRA to do the job of producing a film about its work, and that film was shown throughout the world, just as most of the national film board's work is shown to-d'ay.
These 30S films I have mentioned are divided into forty-six films of the national film programme, 153 in the war information programme, and 109 for other government departments. I do not suppose any agency of the government has so many connections with other government departments as the film board. It receives orders for films and produces them in cooperation with government departments. We think it produces them as well and perhaps better than any private agency could do it, and it makes a Canadian service continuously available to the government and to the people of Canada. It is with some pride that I speak of this service and' the way in which its reputation has been, built up through the years in consequence of the work that has been carried on, particularly under the leadership of John Grierson, who is known throughout the world as probably the leader in the field of documentary films, and who received the highest award, an Oscar, in the United States, a year ago.
The record is known to the people of every other country, and it is high time that it became known to the people of Canada. More and more people in Canada are beginning to recognize that here is one field of culture, one field of art in. which we can take second place to no other country.
These pictures cover a great range of subjects. The most important series that was shown probably was that of "The World in Action". That series of films produced one each month and was shown as a commercial picture for which we received payment. It was shown in six thousand theatres in the United States and in a great number of theatres in the United Kingdom, in Central and South America as well as in Australia and South Africa. Another series "Canada Carries On", was perhaps the greatest single vehicle for carrying to the Canadian people and to others knowledge of what we ourselves were doing during the war. That was also shown in Canada, the United States and other countries. These two films were shown to an estimated audience in Canada of two million people a week. We get into very 
large figures in this field. That is the potential audience at the theatres in which these films are shown.
I have here, and if necessary and desirable, I shall put on Hansard a list of the 308 films produced during the period under review. A great number of these films are produced in both English and French. A great number were produced in Spanish and Portuguese. I venture to say they have been, the greatest single vehicle for carrying knowledge and information of Canada to other countries.
As part of its work the national film board has also been the greatest single agency in Canada to produce still pictures, pictures of national events. It has had its own photographers on our battle fronts, and they have made available through the ordinary means of distributing information photographs and stills in a very large volume, up to 50.000 a year.
This activity also includes the preparation of graphics of all kinds, educational films, films for the Department of Agriculture and so forth. We have had a great number of rural circuits. They also show films on industrial circuits. The rural circuits and the industrial circuits are means whereby information about farm life and ways of improving the amenities of farm life and farm techniques as well as entertainment are made available to hundreds of thousands of our population. Similarly the industrial circuits make available films on industrial techniques. Some of them are just as practical as any employer could possibly introduce with regard to one element or another suitable to the audience. They also endeavour to spread from one group to another knowledge of the other group, how they are living, how they are working and that they are interdependent. That is all part of the effort to give Canadians information of their own country, a realization of what we are doing and what we aim to do. It is a great Canadian enterprise. On that account I hope that it will get the vote which is required here.
With regard to the question of the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, I must say that the only information I have is that the film to which he refers was probably produced for the air force by an agency other than the film board. If it was found unsuitable that was not their fault.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I should just like to express appreciation on behalf of the tourist bureau of Fort William of the splendid service rendered by the film board. We have a cave surrounded by hard rocks and pretty well covered by evergreens. On a summer evening several hundred people meet in that cave,

Supply-Health and Welfare
tourists from all over the United States. One man expressed himself in words like these: We did not know that you had such a beautiful and gorgeous country as Canada.

speechtext: If the film board is to become really efficient and adequate a great deal will depend upon the number of projectors which are available for groups, clubs and associations. speechtext:
I should like to associate
myself with the compliments that are being paid at the moment to the minister and to the national film board, but I have had brought to my attention a couple of criticisms which may not be justified. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

only films distributed in Canada are distributed in English and French. The films that have been sent out in Spanish and Portuguese are sent to the countries where these languages would be useful.

I understand that perfectly,
but I understood that a considerable number of films were sent out in languages other than the four mentioned.

speechtext: Three years ago we made a film in Ukrainian for distribution in Canada.
