maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I wish to compliment the
minister on the imagination and sympathy which he has shown in dealing with this branch of education. I was pleased when I found that the film board came under his department, although I only became aware of that fact this week. Twice this week I have had the chance of seeing some films the board has produced, together with films produced in other countries, and I wish to say that what the minister said is quite true; the films our own board has made equalled or excelled in technique those from other countries, and I was very glad to see the skill that has gone into the making of those pictures.
In this country, where we have so much space, I believe geography is against us; and in the building of national understanding and unity I think the film is going to play a greater and greater part. I believe it is one of the matters about which we cannot afford to be niggardly, in which we must invest generously, because it is one of the greatest possible mediums for drawing this country together; and now educators are telling us that visual education is by far more effective than any other type. But I think our films can make their greatest contribution in promoting the sort of rural communities that will attract and hold our young people. We have seen those young people drift away from the country, leaving only those older people who perhaps have a greater vision of what life can mean. But if we are to attract these young people back to the farms; if we are to have the sort of culture that we deserve and that these young people are capable of developing in our rural communities, we must make much greater use of this effective medium.
Again I wish to compliment the minister on his sympathy and vision and on the very fine job this branch is doing.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
It would seem that the realism of the east is now up against the idealism of the west. Perhaps we do not go to theatres in the east often enough to appreciate these things. I was glad to hear that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle was able to go to the theatre in Ottawa, because I really have never had time since coming
Supply-Health and Welfare

here, and perhaps I have missed something. This is the position as we see it. We may not be interested in films, but we cannot understand why this amount should be increased by a million dollars. The minister has said that some 153 war pictures were produced, either this year or in preceding years, and no doubt those films were shown to the soldiers overseas. I do not know, but I would suppose that to be the case. What is his method of distribution here in eastern Canada? Are these films available to certain clubs and so on, or are they shown over regular circuits of moving-picture theatres? It strikes me that this amount, instead of getting larger, should be getting smaller, and that unless there is some method of distributing these pictures so that they are shown in the ordinary theatres they are not accomplishing the purpose intended, because my experience in the east has been that these private film shows receive very little attention.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am afraid the minister
has let me down a bit in the remarks I made a while ago; however, I imagine it is all right. I do not feel that I can wax quite as enthusiastic in support of the minister, with respect to the national film board, as some hon. members have done to-night. I have no particular objection to the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North, although I would not be quite so enthusiastic about it and personally I would have modified my remarks if I had thought along the same line.
I agree more or less with the remarks of the hon. member for Saint John-Albert. It is said that the national film board can be a great institution for education. Well, I agree with that, but I do not agree that the educationalists are always right. There are some sciences in the realm of education that cannot oe contradicted. Those sciences are always right, and I have in mind the science of .mathematics and the science of chemistry, for instance. \ ou do not go wrong in those sciences. But when it comes to such matters as political science, political economy and matters of economics, then the educationalists can be wrong, and they have been wrong.
I believe the national film board has a function to perform. I am not going to say that it should be done away with, or anything of the kind. During the war years I believe it diid a good job along certain lines. I have seen some pictures, for instance, dealing with the matter of inflation, that were very good; they were needed at the time, and, I believe, did something in behalf of Canada by helping to curb a little spending and showing people what the dangers of inflation could be. If films are sent abroad in an effort to advertise 
our country, that is an admirable thing. But I am going to throw out a warning, and I do not want it to be suggested or thought that I have a suspicious mind. I am going to say that an institution such as the national film board can become a great power for propaganda. It does not make any difference that the officials in charge say, no, they are going to remain strictly neutral in matters relating to political issues. That is all right; I quite suppose they try to be neutral. But it does not necessarily follow that because certain propaganda does not have a party tinge, therefore it is not political. There are world issues of a highly political nature, not because they favour one party as above another, but because they are issues on which all do not agree. When a medium such as films is used for the purpose of propagandizing a certain view when quite a substantial body of opinion [DOT] is against that view, then I say we need to sound a warning and suggest that the money of the taxpayers should not be used for that sort of thing.
There is another point to it. It is difficult to say where the line should be drawn between what might constitute government propaganda and what might constitute an educational programme. I have enijoyed the films "Canada Carries On". I am not going to say that the film board should not continue in that work. Personally, I do not think it affects me very much; but I will suggest that, no matter what government is in office, there are certain axioms of psychology which cannot be avoided', namely the psychology that when people see "Canada Carries On" there is left within their minds, even though it be their subconscious minds, the thought that the government is doing a great job. I say, therefore, that the national film board should be careful. I believe they are, and I am not going to criticize them harshly in this respect. But I do say that when they issue films of a nature to propagandize some particular policy, they are dealing with matters which I do not think are within their functions as a government film board.
I received through the mail the other day- and I have no doubt other hon. members received similar copies-a certain pamphlet.
I do not intend criticizing its contents. This pamphlet is entitled "World or War", and I have read it with considerable interest. It contains the information that copies may be ordered from the United Nations Society in Canada, and that this pamphlet has been issued by the Canadian information service, and designed by the national film board at Ottawa.

Supply-Health and Welfare
On the inside I find some detailed information respecting the united nations organization which, it says, is open to all peace-loving nations. On its face it looks good. But who knows that the present policy of our government, in following along the lines of the united nations organization, is following along the right line. I am not going to say whether it is or not, whether that decision is the right one.
I suppose the national film board is just as safe under the present minister's administration as it would be under any other; but I do know this, that personally I do not agree with the minister's foreign policy. I see things in a different light, and perhaps it is only natural for me to suppose that while the film board is under the minister's administration, films which go out will not contradict the minister's views on foreign policy, and that perhaps in that regard they will follow along the lines of this pamphlet.
I would not expect it to be otherwise. However, I must repeat that there is a big danger in an institution of this kind. I have said the same about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. There is a danger of institutions like these becoming powerful mediums of propaganda for certain things which in the end may prove detrimental to our country.
Concluding my remarks, I would make this suggestion, that institutions such as the national film board, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, or any other, should come under the closest scrutiny of parliament every year. I would suggest that the appropriate parliamentary committees be set up regularly, so that officials could make their annual reports, and so that those annual reports could be scrutinized from every angle.
This institution may be safe in the hands of the present officials; I do not know. But it may not be safe in the hands of others who may follow in their footsteps. That is the reason why institutions of this kind should come under the closest scrutiny.

I am a believer in films, and I believe in them particularly because of what has been said by the hon. members for Qu'Appelle and Winnipeg North. Nevertheless I think there is great danger that in the schools we may overuse these new inventions. Teachers have pointed out certain of the dangers they face in schools. They say that their children spend most of their spare time either at the
films or listening to the radio, and it is pointed out that neither of those entails the slightest degree of effort on the part of the child. I believe, therefore, that overuse of films could be a detriment in education.
As I said, I am a believer in films. But, like all new things, they can get the bit in their teeth, and run away with themselves.
I cordially welcome what has been said by way of suggestion by the hon. member for Macleod. As a matter of fact, I was going to put forward something of the kind, but the hon. member has done it better than I could have done. However, I suggest earnestly to the minister that something of that kind should be done at the next session.
I am not going to take the time of the committee to discuss this in detail this evening, but I wish to make one other comment, which has to do with a great many things. Much as I believe in the films, I had thought that perhaps they would not be used to the same extent that might have been necessary in war time. I confess, therefore, I was surprised to find the expenses in this connection up by about *132,000 in the main estimates, and, reading the supplementary estimates, I am even more surprised to find an additional amount of *335,000 under this item. In other words, this service will cost about fifty per cent more during the next year than it did last year. Those are the figures as I understand them.
All this may be perfectly right, but in my opinion it has become far too easy to get a vote of hundreds of thousands of dollars without anyone spending five minutes to tell us what it is all about. In Muskoka-Ontario $500,000 is a lot of money, and I feel that before this passes in a perfunctory way, as it seems in danger of doing, we should know where this $500,000 is going.
As I understand it, Mr. Grierson has developed this thing in a big way. He was the pioneer, and was a man who had great ability along this line. May I endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Macleod. I should like to say in that connection that I believe the United States congress has recently passed a law under which a great many corporations and other governmental administrative bodies which formerly reported only to various ministers of the government of that country now report directly to congress or to a committee of congress.
The amount of money appropriated for the national film board has been mentioned. I think it is $1,140,000 for the year now rapidly passing out. The minister has said that some of these films have been exhibited commercially both here and in other countries, and I should like to know how much has been taken in by way of revenue so that we may get some idea of the scope of the activities of the national film board,
I must say that the films of the national film board that I have seen have not left a very favourable impression upon my mind.
I have seen some of their documentary films; then, shortly after, I have seen corresponding productions of United States film companies, and certainly there is no comparison between the two. I remember one film put out by this board called "Balkan Powder Keg". That film outraged the sensibilities of thousands of my constituents to such an extent that it had not been showing for more than a day or two before my telephone was bombarded with demands that it be withdrawn. I immediately telephoned Mr. LaFleche, who was then in charge of this branch of government, and he said that an investigation would be made but that for the time being he did not see that the film need be withdrawn. This film, "Balkan Powder Keg", was definitely antiBritish, not so much by direct picturization as by innuendo. It depicted that the worst wars always started in the Balkans, and it was distinctly pro-Russian and anti-British. It certainly engendered -real opposition in the minds of the people of Toronto. I daresay the minister was flooded with other protests, and shortly afterward he wrote me a nice letter saying that this particular film product of the board, "Balkan Powder Keg", had been withdrawn from circulation. I hope it has stayed withdrawn.
, While some of these films may be exhibited in the United States, I do not know exactly what object they are achieving to advertise our country there. We have an extremely able press, an illustrated press as well, and 
there are correspondents of the great United States journals in Ottawa and in other parts of Canada. These men can tell the United States public what we do in Canada. If the minister could do something to stop the flow of good Canadian citizens across the border from my own city and1 from other places in Canada he would be doing a greater service to our country than by trying to advertise Canada in foreign lands.
While some things may have an element of goodness in them, and this may be one of them, there is a limit to the amount of money that we can spend. Every time we spend money we not only take certain of our people out of productive service who would otherwise be producing other goods and services for Canadians, but we saddle on the backs of those of us who still remain producers an extra tax burden, a burden which is becoming so heavy that if it is not lightened we certainly shall see a diminution of the forward progress of this country and an increase in unemployment.

On every day of every week, every afternoon until perhaps eleven o'clock, the theatres of this country are open. You can go downtown in Ottawa or in any other city and you will see this process of education going on. The adult and juvenile mind is being exposed to this process. Thousands of films, largely made in other countries, are exhibited, and we have absolutely no control over their production or the ideas they represent or the sort of morals they hold up to us for emulation. They are moulding public opinion through a process of education in this country.
But here we have one agency upon which we spend a niggardly sum; comparatively speaking, it is nothing in our national budget. Here we have the means of putting"out wholesome ideas to which we need to expose the people of this country. Supply-Health and Welfare
One of these dealt with a community service in the form of a library on wheels in British Columbia. It was one of the finest things I have ever seen. I wish we had that service everywhere in Canada. I am sure that the showing of that film will promote interest in that sort of thing in other parts of Canada. People will begin to assume local responsibilities for taking part in that sort of thing. speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, and I am glad that
the leader of the opposition has asked that question because my colleagues do not always fully appreciate the office of Secretary of State. Incidentally it is the oldest portfolio in the history of the country other than that of the post of Prime Minister.
The office of Secretary of State has under it first of all the administration of the companies branch, dealing with the incorporation of companies under dominion charter, which in itself, as the hon. gentleman will well appreciate is an important matter. There is also the registration of trade marks and patents, the correspondence branch which in-

Supply-Secretary of State
eludes registration, under the Trades Union Act, the king's printer, an organization of well over 900 printers and others, in regard to whom I may take this opportunity of making this statement, that during the war they rendered as valuable a service to this country as any group of servants or any other body of workers, with the possible exception of the armed forces, who, of course, bore the primary responsibility of carrying on the war. The printers, the linotype operators and the pressmen work three shifts and even to-day, this staff is working almost beyond human endurance. They deserve the thanks of this house, which I take the liberty of conveying to them on behalf of the house.
Then there is the civil service commission. It does not by statute come under the ministry of the Secretary of State, but by tradition and by custom the Secretary of State has acted as the liaison between the commission and parliament, and the executive arm of government, and I have taken advantage of the opportunity of extending the scope of the minister's functions in that regard. The civil service commission, supervising a personnel now of a little over 143,000, makes the government the largest employer in Canada.
In addition, there is the transfer of a new branch from the Department of National War Services, the citizenship branch, to that of the Secretary of State. Naturalization and' matters affecting the status of aliens and nationality have been dealt with by the office of the Secretary of State. It may interest the committee to know that that is not as perfunctory an organization as it might seem when one considers that no less than a million people who are now nationals in this country have become nationals as a result of the benefits and procedures afforded under the Naturalization Act, and the care of the records of naturalization entails in itself a tremendous task.
Now to that has been added the citizenship branch, a branch of government that was created at the beginning of the war and was intended largely as a means of keeping in contact with all foreign language newspapers in particular and furnishing them with news and the translation of events. That now has been transferred to the office of the Secretary of State, and the intention is to make active use of the citizenship branch, to make it an integral part of the operations, which I trust will come into being when the Citizenship Act is passed by this house.
That in a general way is a survey of the office of Secretary of State.
Then, of course, there is the archives. The archives is one of the oldest branches in the department. It has to do with the preservation of documents both precious and practical, and those that are intended to serve an historical purpose, A new function is being added to the work of the archives by the creation recently by the government of a committee on the conservation of public records. One of the greatest disasters, from the point of view of historical research at the end of the last war, was that the storage of important documents was not adequate, with the result that many documents were lost, so that the writing of history suffered. Consequently an interdepartmental committee, under the chairmanship of the Secretary of State, has been set up to decide what documents shall be destroyed, what documents shall be preserved, and where in any event they shall be distributed. While this may seem to be a minor ministerial act on the face of it, it is an extremely important matter. speechtext: Payments, if that is what the hon. member means.
How much did it cost the government, because of the action in the first place and the restitution?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I shall have to give the particulars at a later date.
Is the custodian of enemy property free to give the committee an account of the property which is under his jurisdiction in that connection?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: As custodian?
Yes.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

As I understand it, not only enemy property is in his custodianship but also property of nationals in enemy occupied countries. Can he give us the figure for the respective former occupied countries in that connection? We are now granting aid to many of these countries. Is it a fact that some of their nationals owned1 valuable securities either representing properties in Canada or the physical paper security in the custodianship of the minister? What is the amount of that? Has the government made any effort to make sure that Canada acquires the securities against aid which may be given to some of these formerly enemy occupied countries?
Supply-Secretary of State

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
With regard to the value of the property under the custodian, the hon. member will understand that there is a difference between par and market value. I hesitate a little even to say this, but I would think that possibly the market value of the property-and this is a very rough estimate- might be close on to one billion dollars. That does not mean that that would be the actual value at the date of the sale or that it is the assessed value. It would all depend on contingencies which my hon. friend no doubt appreciates. I cannot tell him offhand the value of the property of nationals in enemy occupied territory. I was going to hazard a guess, but perhaps I had better not do that.
With regard to the general question that he raised, there is taking place in Paris at the moment-possibly the conference is over now-a sort of preparatory commission leading up to a more general reparations conference, at which conference presumably will be discussed the whole question of reparations arising out of direct damage to property as a result of the war, or as a result of the cost of the war to the countries participating in the conference. The problem would be whether Canada would make a claim for damage to property, which conceivably might be relatively slight, or whether she would simply make a claim for the cost of the war against the enemy. At the moment I can only say that those matters have not been decided. The conference which is now under way is a preliminary one, and we shall have to await the return to Canada of our representatives there, who include a representative of the custodian's office.

That relates to enemy
property. Could the minister say anything about the property owned by nationals of formerly occupied countries?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: That would be all part of the claim. When we come to assess what Canada's reparation claim will be, circumstances of that nature will be borne in mind. The question then to consider will be the control which any individual country may be able to exercise over the assets of the enemy within the possession of the applicant country, in this case Canada; for instance, to what extent would Canada have control of these assets at the end of the war?

The enemy assets of
which we now have control undoubtedly will not go back to the enemy; certainly they will go to make up the reparations.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: That would depend on the general united nations decision.

In connection with the
other class of assets, owned by nationals of enemy occupied countries, surely there will be no claims against them on the part of other countries. But we in Canada are advancing money to some of these countries by way of relief, and I submit that at the same time wealthy nationals of these countries ' should not be allowed to withdraw those securities for their own uses, while Canada, as it were, makes an outright gift. I wish to know if there are substantial assets owned by these nationals of formerly occupied countries, and what the present policy of the government is in regard to their disposition vis-a-vis the gifts or credits we are advancing to these countries.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There are assets, but I can only say that the matter has not reached a state of final decision. It depends upon the circumstances which I just mentioned in a general way.

But you are not releasing
the assets?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I wish to ask one further question, I am not clear with respect to the owners of properties which were taken over by the government early in the war under this arrangement, and some of which I know were sold at figures considered- to be less than their value. I understood from the minister that the former owners had been satisfied in some way. I do not see how they could be satisfied under circumstances like that, unless somebody satisfied them, which would mean unless Canada assisted them. I am not asking the minister for an answer now, but it is a point on which I should like some information, if not now, at least some time. At the moment I am not criticizing the administration; it is just that we do not have the information we think we should have.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I can only say that to the best of my knowledge the parties involved seem to be satisfied. I am not aware that they are not. I had a discussion with them last week in respect of another matter, and some slight reference was made to the former arrangement. I could only assume from the discussion which took place in my office that there was no dissatisfaction.

I have had several letters from Chinese residents of Vancouver who, prior to the outbreak of the Japanese war, bought bank drafts in favour of Chinese benevolent societies. These Chinese tell me that the bank drafts were never delivered in

Supply-Secretary of State
Hong Kong, owing to the fact that war broke out, and now they believe their money should be refunded. I understand that there have been some communications between the government and the banks in connection with this matter. Is there any possibility of these people having their money refunded in the near future?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: This matter will be given the fullest attention and consideration.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
319. Naturalization branch, $65,655.

Have any changes been
made in the naturalization procedure? I know he had in mind introducing more solemnity into the court ceremony, and there was also some talk of setting up schools at which applicants for naturalization could acquire some idea of Canadian history, the Canadian constitution, and the responsibilities of citizenship. Have any steps been taken in that direction?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I am quite aware of the bon. gentleman's interest in these matters and his participation in the discussions of the defence of Canada regulations committee on these very points. One or two of his suggestions have been borne in mind by myself and my officials ever since I have been in the ministry. As the hon. gentleman knows, there is now before parliament a new Citizenship Act, under which authority is given to make regulations in regard to the ceremony of naturalization, and later, under the new act, the ceremony of admission into citizenship, in order to make these much more impressive functions than hitherto has been the case. I can only say that after I became Secretary of State I took the position that some special attention ought to be paid to the delivery of these naturalization certificates, and a carefully prepared letter, a welcoming letter of warmth, of understanding and of cooperation has accompanied every certificate that has gone out. These letters are important, not because they bear my signature, but because they come from a minister of the crown. Last week I took part in a ceremony in Toronto, when some fifty new Canadians were admitted into citizenship. Judge Parker, the senior county court judge of the county of York, who has been perhaps one of the outstanding judges in seeing that these ceremonies have been conducted seriously and impressively, asked me to take part in the ceremonies; the daughters of the empire and other organizations participated and it is the intention of the
Secretary of State in the course of the next year to go right across the country attending these ceremonies, with the idea of seeing if we cannot make them more impressive and more awe-inspiring not only for those becoming Canadian citizens but also for those participating in the ceremonies as sponsors.
It will be the job of this new citizenship branch to assist in doing that very thing. The naturalization branch deals with the issuing of certificates, the filing of certificates and other ministerial acts. Once that has been done, the job of making the ceremony more impressive will be up to the new branch, and that matter is being carefully considered along the general lines I have just indicated.
What about the schools?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The new citizenship branch will work in cooperation with various organizations in the country, including some of the high schools. In the city of Toronto, for instance, night classes are held at certain times of the year by well-intentioned men and women who teach civics and history in these schools, to give the fundamentals of our way of life andi our form of government to these new Canadians. The intention is to prepare a satisfactory manual, in collaboration with national organizations throughout the country, to give these people the essentials and to impress upon them not only the advantages but, as well, the responsibilities of the step they have taken. We are keeping in close touch with many of the organizations of new Canadians, through their publications and so on, and we hope to extend that work along the lines my hon. friend has indicated. I hope, by the end of the next session, after the new act has come into existence, to be able to indicate not only what we intend to do but what we have really succeeded in doing.

The minister has paid tribute to Judge Parker for what he has done in connection with naturalization. I suggest that tribute should also be paid to Mr. Justice Dysart of Winnipeg, who has done excellent work along these lines.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I am informed' Mr. Justice Dysart sent the department a set of recommendations. Probably that was before the present minister took office. Can he tell us about them and whether the department has acted upon them in any way

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I am glad that the hon. member mentioned Mr. Justice Dysart who, in his capacity as a supreme court judge, and
Supply-Secretary oj State

also as one of the officers of the Winnipeg Canadian Club took upon himself the responsibility of giving this matter direction in that city. I am pleased to join with my hon. friend' in paying tribute to Mr. Justice Dysart.
The recommendations he has sent have been carefully considered. Many of them cannot be implemented until the new act comes into being, but some of them have been implemented and, generally speaking, they meet with departmental approval.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
320. Companies branch, $43,095.

I understand that changes have been made in the British companies act, upon which ours is closely modeled. Has the minister given consideration to those recent changes, and does he propose at a subsequent session to incorporate any of them in our Companies Act?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I am hoping that at a subsequent session there will be some revision. I cannot say at this time whether those revisions will include any of the suggestions made in the British act. However, they are being carefully considered.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
322. Bureau for translations, $423,870.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why is there an increase here?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There have been some increases as of two or three months ago, and there will be more, The task imposed upon the bureau for translation is simply tremendous. I am afraid we have overworked' a good many of these translators during the war, particularly, and the job has not eased' up. The creation of some of these new departments has placed upon the bureau for translations a heavy task, and I can only say that this increase is due to increased work.
How many are in the bureau?
The information states hat there are eighty-eight.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There are more than that now, about 180, including the temporaries.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
325. Patent and copyright office; administration division, $35,375.
What is the process followed in having an invention patented?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend will n/ot misunderstand me when I say that the soundest procedure is to consult a good1 lawyer,

and particularly one who has had experience in this type of work. However, the procedure, briefly, is that you send on your specifications or plans to the commissioner and to the department. They are dealt with and examined, in the light of prior claims, special attention being paid to the matter of encroachment. This procedure is technical, and depends upon the type of invention. However, the formula of approach is simple.
Why does the minister think the best approach is through a lawyer? What has a lawyer to do with the matter, when acting as go-between?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
One would wish to make sure that his plan or device is clear and unequivocal. There are men in the legal profession who have had engineering training, and who have special qualifications for drawing plans and giving advice. They can carry on technical discussions with the examiners and other officers of the department.
However, there are hundreds of these applications concerning which no legal advice is given, nor am I suggesting that it should be sought in every case. But in an application which involves a complicated invention, let us say for industrial use, and that sort of thing, it is good advice to have the services of a competent lawyer. As I have said, there are many inventions which do not require that kind of assistance. But, as one goes to a doctor for an appendectomy, one should go to a person qualified to deal with patent applications, when he has a detailed device to be patented.
A very fine book has been issued by the department, which deals completely with the subject.

I do not wish to hold up these estimates, but I must point out that in the last two or three years, in investigations in the United States and Canada an increasing amount of evidence has been brought out respecting the curtailment of trade through the holding of certain patent rights by various companies. I believe that the time has come when we should set up a committee of the house, probably at the next session, to go into this whole matter of patents, and our relationship in international agreements, as applied to patents.
It is time this matter was considered, because we are entering a period when we shall want to 'have freer trade relations with all parts of the world. From the evidence accumulated in the last few years there can be no doubt that the matter of patents has been restricting international trade-and not only

Supply-Labour
international trade, but trade within our own boundaries. Would the minister consider setting up a special committee of the house at _ the next session to consider this whole matter of Canadian patents, and their relationship to international patent agreements?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The administration of this particular division would not, in itself, be concerned with the general problem discussed by the hon. member. Essentially we are a ministerial body carrying out a definite function. But to the extent that this does involve the broader policy may I say that my own sympathies in this matter are not dissimilar to those of the hon. member. I have already taken steps in this connection, and matters are now being studied in circles beyond my own department.

Are there any limitations, under the legislation as it now exists, respecting the length of time a patent can run? Does the department require when such patents shall be used, stipulating that otherwise they will lapse?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, there are such
conditions.
What is the length of time?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It would depend upon the circumstances. However, there are conditions of use.
Covering all patents?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Most patents, yes. It would not cover them all, but, generally speaking, that is correct.
Could the minister give an approximation of the number of patents now in his office?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Call up on the telephone on Monday.
I will call on Tuesday, when the minister's estimates come up-or on Wednesday.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I will give that information to my hon. friend, although I have it with me at the present time.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
579. Companies branch, further amount required, $5,200.
Does this branch result in a net revenue, or after taking off the fees, is it an expense to the government?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The revenue far exceeds the expenditures, and that is true all. through the years.
I take it that the revenue goes directly to the consolidated fund.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Departmental administration, $526,002.

As far as certain phases of its work are concerned, the functions of the Department of Labour will become of increasing importance. We are now in a period of shortage of labour and are back again where we were before the war when we have more applicants for jobs than there are jobs. The latest official report that has come to my hand shows that the unemployment situation at the beginning of October was commencing to get bad. At that time there was a decline of 42,437 persons employed as compared with September 1. The employment situation in all but three of the twenty largest cities of Canada showed a decline in employment on October 1 as compared with September 1.
As far as Vancouver is concerned, employment has been on the decline since October 1, 1944. Some people may not realize this, but the payroll index from October 1, 1944, to October 1, 1945, shows a fall of 10-7 per cent. I am wondering what the policy of the department will be to take care of the unemployment situation and to stop this trend before it goes so far as to cause, not only distress but unrest in various centres of Canada. When we were discussing the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs figures were quoted to show that the situation in Vancouver was extremely critical and likely to cause trouble at any time. Before we adjourn, could the minister give a summary of what the department has in mind to meet this situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows, the Department, of Labour is a placement agency. My hon. friend had ample opportunity to discuss this matter when the estimates of the Department of Reconstruction were being reviewed. I think it will be freely admitted that the placement machinery we have to-day is far better than anything we have had before in the history of this country. I am amazed myself that conditions are somewhat better than some agents of gloom predicted a few months ago they would be. At that time we heard predictions of there being half a million people out of employment by the
Supply-Labour

end of October. When we realize that during the last four months we have placed over
750,000	people in the employment stream it gives some idea of the resiliency of free institutions and the ability of our Canadian economy to absorb people into productive employment.
I am not underestimating the magnitude of the problem; but in view of the sudden collapse of Japan and the almost overnight stoppage of war production, the results achieved so far have been in my opinion-I am speaking as an individual who has watched this situation closely from day to day-much better than the most sanguine people imagined they would be. Let us get back to our machinery. This is a seasonal country. Many years ago my hon. friend and myself advocated the institution of unemployment insurance. That has been established and almost 2,500,000 people come within the orbit of that policy.
This is the time when we get a drop in employment which one looks for in a country of this description. We even had it last year. I remember some of the difficulties with which some of my hon. friends were confronted in the supply of man-power for many of our basic industries. I am not one of those who are fearful of the future. I believe that the Canadian economy is in as sound shape as any other economy I know of to face up to the inevitable situation. In Great Britain they still have close to 4,000,000 people in the armed forces, and at the moment they have an unemployment situation of about 100,000. It is what one might call a book item.
My. hon. friend spoke of Vancouver, and I should like to say this about that situation. Like all cities in which one does not experience the rigours of climate that we have in the central and northeastern parts of America, it is inevitable that there be a shift of population toward that city. I do not know what one can do about it when freedom of movement is guaranteed to any individual in this country. It is just one of those things that are done in every country where these extreme conditions exist. We had it in prewar days, and we had it in considerable measure during the war period when people from the prairie provinces went to the coast, just as they do in the United States to get away from the rigours of the climate. I am not an alarmist. I do not take a negative attitude on questions of this kind. I have expressed this opinion before, that provided we can maintain a stable price level and get the cooperation of the people of this dominion and, of course, a reasonable stability in international trade which is of great importance to

a country where two out of every five persons rely upon export trade for opportunities for employment-

Two out of every five
depending on exports?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Yes, I think that is
correct.
Correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Two out of every five,
speaking from memory.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think it is three out of
eight.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: That is approximately the same. When we get that and a proper distribution of labour in this country I am hopeful that some of the predictions of the calamity howlers will disappear. That is a prediction.

It is a hope.
Mr. MITCHELL.:	Just wait a minute.
You should not call me that.
I did not call you anything. I said it is a hope, not a prediction.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
That is just like the
speech the hon. member made the other day in regard to stabilizing the price level. If my hon. friend wants to discuss that I shall be glad to discuss it with him at some other time. The government should be given some credit for the contribution we have made in this war when the situation was very dark and we stood alone. We should be given credit for sincerity in our approach to the problems that faced us. My hon. friend in his speech only yesterday-paradoxical, it is true-said that this had been the ablest government in the country and that this was the ablest parliament in his memory. We are in the soup together, and that is why I like parliament. That is why I think there is nothing better. My hon. friend laughs.

I am laughing because
you like parliament because we are all in the soup together.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
A good bowl of soup
would probably do my hon. friend no harm.
I like parliament because you get criticism, which is the lifeblood of democracy, and notwithstanding all the good things my hon. friend said about the ability of the government I still think we can learn from the opposition and even from himself.

Prime Minister-Birthday Greetings
That is rather remote.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
You said that; I did
not.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: topic
Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the consent of the house I would move a motion which I have already discussed with the various groups. I move:
That when the house adjourns this day it stands adjourned until Monday next at eleven o'clock, and that the house do sit through Monday without recess until six p.m., and from eight p.m. until midnight or until such earlier *time as the business of the house is concluded, and that standing orders 2, 6 and 7 be suspended in relation thereto.

At the rate at which
we have been proceeding to-day and yesterday I hesitate to support the motion for fear that we might be here until Wednesday or Thursday. Could we not leave the motion over until Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The only alteration it makes is that we sit during the luncheon recess.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I thought the motion
was to allow the house to carry on until three or four o'clock in the morning.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, until midnight, if we do not conclude the business earlier.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is an invitation
that we hurry up and get through early.

Since this motion
means that we are going to sit without the noon recess, I think we should be given the order in which the various departments and other business will be taken up and that that schedule should be adhered to.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have that here and
will give it when moving the adjournment of the house.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to.
Mr. MACKENZIE moved the adjournment of the house.
He said:	At eleven o'clock on Monday
morning the Prime Minister will proceed with the resolution in regard to atomic energy and then with his estimates on external affairs and the various other estimates in relation to the Prime Minister's departments. When we dispose of that we shall take up in this order; Fisheries, the Department of Labour, Post Office and Public Works, Finance, which includes the auditor general; Transport, Reconstruction and Munitions and Supply are all together to be handled by the Minister of Transport:	National Defence; legislation,
under the jurisdiction of Mr. Speaker; National Revenue. That is the order so far as it can be followed.

Might I suggest that if
we proceed on this schedule there should be a wide discussion allowed on the items? We cannot sit all day without nourishment, and the result is that a member may come back and find that the item he is interested in has been passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I think the various
groups and parties can easily arrange relays of those who want to be in the house and the rest can have a lunch outside.

The trouble is that the
other man cannot make my speech and I cannot make his.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I realize the impossibility of the situation.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 11.50 p.m.
Monday, December 17, 1945.
